sections.title: FIN-M04-L02: UPI, cards and net banking: using them safely
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use UPI, cards and net banking with safe habits, know your rights when money is taken without your permission, and have a written plan for the first hour after a fraud. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 65 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

UPI made payments in India fast and free. It also made fraud fast. Almost every payment fraud works by tricking **you** into approving a payment or sharing a code; the technology itself is rarely broken. So safety is mostly a set of habits.

### Five UPI facts that stop most frauds

1. **Your UPI PIN is only for paying money out.** You never need it to receive money. Anyone who says "enter your PIN to receive the refund" is a fraudster.
2. **Scanning a QR code is for paying.** A QR code never brings money in.
3. **A "collect request" asks you to pay.** Read every request before approving it; decline anything you didn't expect.
4. **Never share OTPs, PINs or passwords,** and never install a screen-sharing app because a caller asks you to. Banks, RBI, the police and courier companies never ask.
5. **Check the name before you pay.** UPI shows the registered name of the receiver. If it doesn't match who you think you are paying, stop.

### Cards and net banking

- Use your bank's app or type the bank's address yourself; don't search for it and click an ad. Banks in India moved their websites to addresses ending in **.bank.in**, which only regulated banks can use; RBI asked banks to complete the move by 31 October 2025 ([Business Standard, April 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/news/rbi-asks-banks-to-complete-migration-to-bank-in-domain-by-october-31-2025-125042201515_1.html)).
- Use the card controls in your bank app: turn off international and online use when you don't need them, and set limits.
- Keep SMS and email alerts on, and read them. An alert you ignore is a fraud you discover late.
- Don't save cards on websites you rarely use.

### Your rights: the RBI liability rules

RBI's rules ([RBI, July 2017](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/FS_Notification.aspx?Id=11040), check current rules) decide who pays when money leaves your account without your permission:

| Situation | Your liability |
| --- | --- |
| The bank's fault (its system, staff or fraud) | Zero, whether or not you reported it |
| A third party's fraud (not you, not the bank), reported within 3 working days of the alert | Zero |
| Same, reported in 4 to 7 working days | Limited: up to ₹5,000 for BSBD accounts, ₹10,000 for other savings accounts and credit cards with limits up to ₹5 lakh, ₹25,000 for others (or the transaction amount, if lower) |
| You were negligent, for example you shared your OTP or PIN | You bear the loss until you report it; the bank covers losses after your report |

The bank must credit the disputed amount to your account (a "shadow reversal") within 10 working days of your report and resolve the complaint within 90 days. The lesson is simple: **report within hours, not days.**

### The first hour after a fraud

1. **Call 1930,** the national cyber crime helpline, available 24 hours ([Kerala Police](https://ps.keralapolice.gov.in/ernakulamruralcyber-ps/notifications/National-Cyber-Crime-Reporting-Helpline-No-1930-3338)). Fast reporting gives police the best chance to freeze the money in the fraudster's account.
2. **Block** your card or UPI through the bank app or the bank's official helpline, and report the transaction to the bank.
3. **Report online** on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, [cybercrime.gov.in](https://cybercrime.gov.in/), and keep the acknowledgement number.
4. **Write to your bank** with the details and keep a copy. If the bank rejects your complaint or doesn't reply within 30 days, complain free to the RBI Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in under the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026, which can award up to ₹30 lakh for loss plus up to ₹3 lakh for harassment ([scheme features](https://www.canarabank.bank.in/documents/d/guest/salient-features-of-the-scheme-2026), check current rules).

## Local example

**Joseph**, Anu's 66-year-old neighbour, received an SMS: "Dear consumer, your electricity will be disconnected tonight at 9.30 pm as your last bill was not updated. Call this number immediately." The caller was polite, said he was "from the electricity office", and asked Joseph to install an app "to update the bill" and pay ₹10.

Joseph's daughter had shown him Anu's fraud response card a month earlier. Two things stopped him: the caller wanted him to install an app (screen sharing), and the message created **urgency**. He hung up, checked his bill in the official way, and found nothing was due.

Anu then helped him set up three safety habits: SMS alerts on every transaction, a daily UPI limit lower than his pension, and the fraud response card stuck inside his kitchen cupboard, with 1930 written in large numbers.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [RBI: customer liability in unauthorised electronic transactions](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/FS_Notification.aspx?Id=11040) | The customer liability table and the timelines (3 days, 4 to 7 days, shadow credit in 10 days) | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala Police: 1930, the national cyber crime helpline](https://ps.keralapolice.gov.in/ernakulamruralcyber-ps/notifications/National-Cyber-Crime-Reporting-Helpline-No-1930-3338) | What the 1930 helpline and the reporting portal are for | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Canara Bank: features of the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026 (PDF)](https://www.canarabank.bank.in/documents/d/guest/salient-features-of-the-scheme-2026) | How to complain to the RBI Ombudsman, and when | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Business Standard: banks to move to the bank.in domain by 31 October 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/news/rbi-asks-banks-to-complete-migration-to-bank-in-domain-by-october-31-2025-125042201515_1.html) | Why bank websites now end in .bank.in (headline) | 2 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 (headline checked) |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. In your bank app, turn on SMS and email alerts for every transaction if they aren't on already.
2. Open the card controls: turn off international use, and online use if you don't shop online. Set a daily limit that fits your spending.
3. Check your UPI app: remove linked accounts you don't use, and check your UPI ID and the name it shows.
4. Save your bank's official helpline number in your contacts, from the bank's own website or passbook.
5. Fill in the fraud response card from the template, print it or save it as a photo, and share it with one family member.
6. Do the 10-question payment safety check with a family member and talk through any "no" answers.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of transaction alerts on and card controls set (cover card numbers), and your fraud response card, saved in 04 Banking.

## Template: fraud response card

```
IF MONEY GOES WITHOUT MY PERMISSION, IN THE FIRST HOUR:
1. Call 1930 (national cyber crime helpline, 24 hours)
2. Block card/UPI in the bank app, or call my bank: ____ (official number)
3. Report at cybercrime.gov.in and write down the acknowledgement number
4. Email/visit my bank in writing; keep a copy
5. If no reply in 30 days or rejected: RBI Ombudsman, cms.rbi.org.in (free)
NEVER: share OTP, PIN or password; install an app because a caller asks; scan a QR code to receive money
```

## Template: 10-question payment safety check

```
1. Transaction alerts on for every account?                        Yes / No
2. Mobile number current in every account?                        Yes / No
3. Card controls set (international off, limits)?                 Yes / No
4. Do I know my UPI PIN is never needed to receive money?         Yes / No
5. Do I check the receiver's name before paying?                  Yes / No
6. Bank's official helpline saved from the official site?         Yes / No
7. Do I open the bank website by typing its .bank.in address?     Yes / No
8. Screen lock and app lock on the phone?                         Yes / No
9. Would I hang up on a caller asking for an OTP, even "from the bank"? Yes / No
10. Does my family know about 1930?                               Yes / No
```

## Common mistakes

- **Thinking "I am too smart to be fooled".** Fraudsters use urgency, fear and authority; educated people lose money every day. Habits protect you when you are tired or scared.
- **Waiting to report "in case it comes back".** Your liability depends on how fast you report. Report within hours.
- **Searching for "customer care" numbers online.** Fake numbers appear in search results and ads. Use the number on the bank's own website, app or passbook.
- **Keeping alerts off to avoid "too many messages".** Alerts are how you catch fraud in minutes instead of weeks.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Someone says you must enter your UPI PIN to receive a refund. What is true?
    - A) You need the PIN for refunds above ₹1,000
    - B) Only on weekends
    - C) You never need a UPI PIN to receive money; it is a fraud
    - D) Only for refunds from banks
2. A third party steals money from your savings account and you report it on the same day. Your liability under RBI rules?
    - A) Zero
    - B) ₹25,000
    - C) The full amount
    - D) ₹10,000
3. What is 1930?
    - A) RBI's head office number
    - B) A bank's customer care
    - C) The income tax helpline
    - D) The national cyber crime helpline
4. Your bank rejected your fraud complaint. Where can you complain next, free?
    - A) Nowhere
    - B) Social media only
    - C) The RBI Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in
    - D) A loan app
5. What is the safest way to open your bank's website?
    - A) Type its official address, which ends in .bank.in
    - B) Ask a caller for the link
    - C) Use a link from an SMS
    - D) Click the first search ad

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** RBI's customer liability rules, the 1930 helpline, the RBI Ombudsman scheme and the .bank.in change
- **Action:** Turn on alerts and card controls, fill in your fraud response card and do the safety check with family. It is done when your proof is saved: screenshots of transaction alerts on and card controls set (cover card numbers), and your fraud response card, saved in 04 Banking.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** The UPI PIN only authorises payments going out of your account.
2. **A.** Third-party fraud reported within 3 working days means zero liability.
3. **D.** It is the 24-hour helpline for reporting cyber and financial fraud.
4. **C.** The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme handles complaints after the bank rejects them or doesn't reply in 30 days.
5. **A.** Ads and SMS links can lead to fake sites; .bank.in is reserved for banks.

sections.title: FIN-M04-L03: FDs, RDs and where to park money
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Calculate the maturity value of an FD and an RD, compare banks and post office deposits on rate, safety, tax and penalties, and choose where short-term money should wait. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Money you need within about three years, such as your emergency fund, sinking funds and short goals, should be **safe and easy to reach**, not chasing high returns. Fixed and recurring deposits are the usual home for it.

### Fixed deposits (FDs)

You deposit a lump sum for a fixed period at a fixed rate.

- **Rates differ** by bank, tenure and type of depositor (senior citizens usually get more). Small finance banks often pay more than large banks; their deposits have the same DICGC cover up to ₹5 lakh.
- **Cumulative FD:** interest is added to the deposit, usually every quarter, and paid at maturity. **Payout FD:** interest is paid monthly or quarterly, useful for retirees like Joseph and Mary.
- **Breaking an FD early** usually costs a penalty on the interest. Check the bank's rule before you deposit.
- **Tax:** FD interest is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate. Banks deduct TDS when your interest from that bank crosses a yearly limit, ₹50,000 for most people and higher for senior citizens ([Finance Bill 2026 notes](https://incometaxindia.gov.in/Budgets%20and%20Bills/2026/Notes-on-clauses-2026.pdf), check current rules). If your total income is below the taxable limit, you can give the bank a self-declaration so it doesn't deduct TDS (known as Form 15G, or 15H for seniors, under the old law; ask the bank for the current form).

**Worked example: cumulative FD with quarterly compounding**

> Maturity = deposit × (1 + rate ÷ 4) ^ (4 × years)

₹50,000 for 3 years at 7% a year: ₹50,000 × (1 + 0.07/4)^12 = **₹61,572**, so interest of ₹11,572. Simple interest would have given ₹10,500; the extra ₹1,072 is compounding.

### Recurring deposits (RDs)

You deposit a fixed amount every month for a fixed period; the bank pays interest on each instalment. RDs suit **sinking funds and goals**: ₹1,000 a month for a festival, a premium or a two-wheeler down payment. A post office RD runs for 5 years and paid **6.7%** a year in October to December 2026 ([India Post](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving), check current rules). Bank RDs come in many lengths.

### Post office time deposits

Post office time deposits (TDs) of 1, 2, 3 and 5 years paid **6.9% to 7.5%** in October to December 2026, set by the government every quarter ([quarterly rates](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/), check current rules). They are backed by the Government of India. FIN-M09-L03 covers all the small savings schemes.

### Where should money wait?

| When you need it | Where it can wait | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| This month | Savings account | Instant access |
| In 1 to 12 months | FD or RD in a bank you trust, or a post office deposit | Safe, a bit more interest, small penalty if broken |
| In 1 to 3 years | FDs, RDs, post office deposits; Module 9 adds other options | Safety still matters more than return |
| More than 3 to 5 years away | Module 9: a mix that can beat inflation | Time to recover from ups and downs |

### Comparing deposits

Compare four things, not just the rate: **safety** (bank type, DICGC cover, how much you already have there), **rate** for your exact tenure, **flexibility** (penalty for early withdrawal), and **tax** (interest is taxed at your slab; post-tax return is what you keep).

## Local example

**Joseph and Mary**, the retired couple next door, kept ₹8 lakh in one FD at a co-operative society because "the secretary is from our church and the rate is half a percent higher". Anu showed them two things: a co-operative society that is not a licensed bank has no DICGC cover ([RBI caution](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=52595)), and even at a bank, cover is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.

They decided, together with their son, to move the deposit at maturity: ₹4 lakh in an FD in Joseph's name at one bank, ₹3 lakh in Mary's name at another, and ₹1 lakh in a post office time deposit, with monthly interest payouts for their expenses. Their interest fell by about ₹1,500 a year. In exchange, every rupee was within deposit insurance or backed by the government. "We sleep better," Mary said.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [India Post: saving schemes and current interest rates](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving) | Current post office interest rates for RD, TD and the other schemes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Indian Bank: small savings interest rates, October to December 2026](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/) | The October to December 2026 small savings rates table | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [DICGC: deposit insurance, what is covered (PDF)](https://website.dicgc.org.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/DICGC_Flyer_0.pdf) | Revise what deposit insurance covers | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Finance Bill 2026: notes on clauses (PDF): due dates, late fee, TDS](https://incometaxindia.gov.in/Budgets%20and%20Bills/2026/Notes-on-clauses-2026.pdf) | Optional: the clause on TDS on interest (search the PDF for "interest") | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Pick a deposit amount and period that fits one of your short goals or sinking funds.
2. Find the current rate for that period at three places: your own bank, one other bank, and the post office (rates are on their official websites or at the branch).
3. Fill in the deposit comparison template with rate, maturity value (by formula), penalty rule, deposit insurance or government backing, and tax note.
4. Decide where your sinking funds and emergency fund money will wait. Write one sentence for each.
5. Optional, only if you have the money and it fits your plan: open the RD or FD you chose. ₹100 to ₹500 is enough to learn the steps.

**Proof to record:** Your filled-in deposit comparison with formulas and your one-sentence decisions (and a screenshot of any deposit opened, numbers covered), saved in 04 Banking.

## Template: deposit comparison (formulas work in both apps)

```
Row 1: Where,Type (FD/RD/post office TD),Rate (e.g. 0.07),Years,Deposit or monthly amount (₹),Maturity value (₹),Interest earned (₹),Early-withdrawal penalty,Insured or govt-backed?,Notes
FD, quarterly compounding (row 2):  F2: =E2*(1+C2/4)^(4*D2)        G2: =F2-E2
RD, approximate value with monthly deposits (row 3):  F3: =FV(C3/12,D3*12,-E3,0,1)   G3: =F3-E3*D3*12
(Banks compound RD interest quarterly, so their maturity figure may differ slightly from this FV approximation; use the bank's calculator to confirm.)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing only on the highest rate.** Half a percent extra is worth little if the deposit isn't insured or you can't withdraw it in an emergency.
- **Putting more than ₹5 lakh in one bank without thinking.** Spread larger amounts across banks or government schemes if safety matters to you.
- **Forgetting tax on interest.** FD interest is taxed at your slab. Compare what you keep, not just the rate.
- **Locking emergency money in long FDs.** Use shorter deposits or a ladder (Module 5) so you can reach it without big penalties.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. ₹50,000 in a 3-year FD at 7% compounded quarterly. Which formula gives the maturity value?
    - A) =50000+7*3
    - B) =50000/(1+0.07)^3
    - C) =50000*(1+0.07/4)^(4*3)
    - D) =50000*0.07*3
2. How is FD interest taxed?
    - A) Added to your income and taxed at your slab rate
    - B) Only if the FD is in a co-operative bank
    - C) At a flat 30%
    - D) Always tax-free
3. What suits a sinking fund for an Onam budget, saved monthly?
    - A) A 10-year FD
    - B) A recurring deposit
    - C) A gold loan
    - D) Shares
4. What was the post office RD rate for October to December 2026?
    - A) 4% a year
    - B) 6.7% a year
    - C) 8.2% a year
    - D) 12% a year

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Current post office and small savings rates, deposit insurance and (optionally) the TDS clause
- **Action:** Compare an FD or RD at three places with formulas and decide where your short-term money will wait. It is done when your proof is saved: your filled-in deposit comparison with formulas and your one-sentence decisions (and a screenshot of any deposit opened, numbers covered), saved in 04 Banking.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Quarterly compounding: rate ÷ 4, and 4 × years compounding periods.
2. **A.** Interest is income; TDS is only an advance part of the tax.
3. **B.** An RD takes fixed monthly amounts and matures when you need the money.
4. **B.** India Post listed 6.7% for the RD in that quarter (check current rates).

sections.title: Module 5: Emergency fund
sections.summary: Decide how big your emergency fund should be, where it should wait, and start building it this week with an automatic transfer.
sections.content:
## Overview

An emergency fund is boring and it changes everything. It turns a hospital bill, a lost client or a flooded kitchen from a debt crisis into an inconvenience. It is also what lets you take sensible risks later, because you won't be forced to sell investments or pledge gold at a bad moment.

This module sizes your fund on your real essential expenses from Module 3, sets a starter target and a full target, puts the money in safe places you can reach quickly, and starts the monthly transfer. It is one of the eight parts of your final plan, and your first monthly money review falls this week too.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain what counts as an emergency and what doesn't
- Calculate essential monthly expenses and choose a starter and a full target
- Choose safe, quick-to-reach places for the fund, including an FD ladder
- Set up an automatic monthly transfer and calculate months to target
- Write rules for using and refilling the fund

## Time

About 4 hours in total: 3 hours of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: week 9.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M05-L01: How big should your emergency fund be? (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. FIN-M05-L02: Where to keep it and how to build it (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Module project: My emergency fund plan, with the first deposit made

1. Complete the Emergency tab: essential expenses, months, starter and full targets, layers, monthly transfer and months to target.
2. Write your emergency rules and refill rule at the top of the tab.
3. Show that the first transfer has happened and the standing instruction is set.
4. Tell one family member where the fund is and what it is for, so they don't treat it as spare money.
5. Add the emergency fund balance to your Net Worth and Review tabs.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of the completed Emergency tab and the standing instruction (numbers covered), saved in 05 Emergency.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size | A guess | Based on income | Based on essential expenses and your income stability |
| Targets | None | One target | Starter and full targets with months to reach each |
| Place | Spending account | Separate but all in one place | Layers: cash, instant account and a ladder, within insurance limits |
| Automation | None | Planned | Standing instruction set and first transfer made |
| Rules | None | In your head | Written use and refill rules |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Calculate essential expenses × months (FIN-M05-L01).
- Open or choose a separate account and set a monthly standing instruction, any amount (FIN-M05-L02).
- Make the first transfer today.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Emergency fund size | Essential monthly expenses × months (3 to 12, depending on how stable your income is). |
| Starter fund | About one month of essential expenses, built first. |
| Three rules for where it waits | Safe, reachable within a day or two, separate from spending. |
| FD ladder | Several small FDs maturing at different times, so you break only what you need. |
| Months to target, no interest | (Target − saved) ÷ monthly saving. |
| NPER in this course | =NPER(rate/12, -monthly, -saved, target) gives months to a target with interest. |
| Emergency test | Urgent, necessary and unexpected: all three must be yes. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Skipping the fund to invest sooner.** Without it, the first shock forces you to sell investments or borrow at high interest.
- **Mixing the fund with sinking funds.** Known yearly costs have their own sinking funds; the emergency fund is only for shocks.
- **Forgetting to refill after using it.** Refill first, then restart other goals.

sections.title: FIN-M05-L01: How big should your emergency fund be?
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Work out your essential monthly expenses and choose a starter target and a full target for your emergency fund, based on how stable your income is. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

An **emergency fund** is money kept aside only for real emergencies: losing your income, illness or an accident, an urgent repair, a family crisis. It is the foundation of every plan in this course. Without it, the first shock pushes you into a credit card, a loan app or a gold loan, and your goals stop.

### What counts as an emergency

- **Yes:** job or income loss, hospital costs insurance doesn't cover, an accident, urgent house repairs after heavy rain, a family emergency far away, a broken phone or laptop you need for work.
- **No:** festivals, weddings, a sale, a new phone you want, a trip, school fees. Those are known costs: they belong in sinking funds (Module 3) or goals (Module 2).

### Size it on essential expenses, not income

Your **essential monthly expenses** are what you must pay even in a crisis: needs from your budget, loan EMIs, insurance premiums (as a monthly amount), and the family support you can't stop. Wants are cut in an emergency, so they are left out.

> **Full emergency fund = essential monthly expenses × number of months**

### How many months?

| Your situation | Suggested months | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permanent salaried job, two incomes in the family | 3 months | Income is stable; another earner can help |
| Salaried job, single income, or dependants | 6 months | More people rely on one income |
| Freelance, tuition, commission or seasonal income | 6 to 12 months | Slow months and gaps between clients are normal |
| Own business, or the only earner in a large family | 9 to 12 months | Business shocks can hit income and savings together |
| Student or PSC aspirant with little income | Start with 1 month, then 3 | Small, steady progress matters most |

These are rules of thumb, not laws. A government job is stable, but illness still costs money; a freelancer with three steady clients is safer than one with a single big client.

### A starter fund first

A full fund can take a year or more to build. So set two targets:

1. **Starter fund:** one month of essential expenses, or a round number like ₹10,000 to ₹25,000. This handles most small shocks. Build it before anything except paying essential bills.
2. **Full fund:** the months from the table. Build it after the starter fund, alongside paying off expensive debt (Module 6).

### Insurance and the emergency fund work together

Health insurance (Module 7) covers big hospital bills; the emergency fund covers what insurance doesn't: co-payments, items not covered, waiting periods, travel and lost income while you recover. Insurance lets your emergency fund be smaller; it doesn't replace it.

### Worked examples (made-up numbers)

- **Anu:** essential expenses ₹9,000; irregular income, so 6 months = **₹54,000**; starter fund **₹9,000**.
- **Rahul:** essential expenses ₹16,500 (including help to his parents); permanent job, single income, parents depend on him, so 6 months = **₹99,000**.
- **Fathima:** essential expenses ₹20,000; freelance, so 9 months = **₹1,80,000**, plus her separate business buffer from FIN-M03-L04.

## Local example

**Rahul** first thought his emergency fund could be small: "It's a government job; the salary will come." Then he listed what had happened in his extended family in the last three years: his father's knee surgery (partly covered by insurance, with ₹38,000 of extras), roof repairs after a heavy monsoon (₹22,000), and his cousin losing a Gulf job and needing help for four months.

None of these was a job loss for Rahul himself, but each one needed money within days. He decided on 6 months of essential expenses, ₹99,000, with a starter fund of ₹16,500. He also noticed something about his old habit: in each of those three events, the family had pledged gold for a loan. "The emergency fund is what lets the gold stay in the locker," his mother said.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The e-LMS module on safety nets and insurance | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. From your Budget tab, add up your essential monthly expenses: needs, EMIs, monthly share of insurance premiums and the family support you can't stop.
2. Choose your number of months from the table, and write one sentence on why.
3. Calculate your starter fund and your full fund.
4. Make an **Emergency** tab with the template and fill in the target section.
5. Write your list of what counts as an emergency for you, and what doesn't.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of the target section of your Emergency tab (essential expenses, months, starter and full targets) and your emergency/not-emergency list, saved in 05 Emergency.

## Template: Emergency tab: targets

```
B2: essential monthly expenses (₹)      (needs + EMIs + premiums/12 + family support you can't stop)
B3: months chosen                        (3, 6, 9 or 12)
B4: full fund target  =B2*B3
B5: starter fund      =B2               (or a round amount)
B6: saved so far (₹)
B7: % of full target  =IF(B4>0,B6/B4*100,0)
B8: starter done?     =IF(B6>=B5,"Yes","Not yet")
```

## Template: my emergency rules

```
IT IS AN EMERGENCY IF: income stops / illness or accident / urgent repair / family crisis / a tool I need for work breaks
IT IS NOT AN EMERGENCY IF: festival / wedding / sale / trip / a gadget I want / a known yearly bill
Before I use it, I ask: is it urgent, necessary and unexpected? All three must be yes.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Sizing it on income instead of essential expenses.** In a crisis you cut wants. Size the fund on what you must still pay.
- **Waiting until the full fund is possible.** Start with a small starter fund now. ₹5,000 handles many small shocks.
- **Thinking a government job needs no emergency fund.** Illness, family crises and repairs don't check your job type.
- **Counting gold as the emergency fund.** Using gold means a loan or a sale at a bad moment. Keep cash savings for emergencies.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Essential expenses are ₹12,000 a month and you choose 6 months. What is the full emergency fund?
    - A) ₹36,000
    - B) ₹72,000
    - C) ₹1,44,000
    - D) ₹12,000
2. Which of these is a real emergency?
    - A) A sale on phones
    - B) A hospital bill not covered by insurance
    - C) Onam shopping
    - D) A friend's wedding gift
3. Who usually needs the most months of expenses saved?
    - A) Everyone needs exactly 3 months
    - B) A freelancer or business owner with irregular income
    - C) A person in a permanent job with two family incomes
    - D) Nobody needs an emergency fund with insurance
4. Why build a starter fund first?
    - A) Banks require it
    - B) It handles most small shocks while you build the full fund
    - C) It earns the highest interest
    - D) It replaces insurance

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The NCFE module on safety nets and insurance
- **Action:** Calculate your essential expenses and set starter and full emergency fund targets in the Emergency tab. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of the target section of your Emergency tab (essential expenses, months, starter and full targets) and your emergency/not-emergency list, saved in 05 Emergency.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** ₹12,000 × 6 = ₹72,000.
2. **B.** Festivals, sales and gifts are known or optional costs, not emergencies.
3. **B.** Irregular income has more gaps and shocks.
4. **B.** A small fund now beats a perfect fund someday.

sections.title: FIN-M05-L02: Where to keep it and how to build it
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Choose safe, quick-to-reach places for your emergency fund, set up an automatic monthly transfer, and calculate how many months it will take to reach your target. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Three rules for where the money waits

1. **Safe:** the amount must not fall. No shares, crypto, chitties or "schemes".
2. **Reachable within a day or two:** emergencies don't wait for an FD to mature.
3. **Separate from spending money:** if it sits in your everyday account, it gets spent.

### A simple three-layer setup

| Layer | How much | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Cash at home | A small amount, say ₹2,000 to ₹5,000 | Somewhere safe at home | For when the network, UPI or ATMs are down, as happens during floods |
| 2. Instant money | About one month of essential expenses | A separate savings account, ideally at a different bank from your spending account, with no card for daily use | Reachable today |
| 3. The rest | The remaining months | FDs at banks you trust, in a ladder, within the ₹5 lakh deposit insurance limit per bank | A bit more interest; reachable in a day by breaking one FD |

**An FD ladder** means splitting layer 3 into several smaller FDs with different maturity dates, for example every three months. If you need ₹20,000, you break one small FD, not the whole fund, and pay a small penalty on that one only. When an FD matures and you don't need it, renew it at the end of the ladder.

Some banks offer an **auto-sweep** facility, where money above a limit in your savings account moves into an FD automatically and comes back when needed. Ask your bank whether it offers this and what it costs. Later, once you understand them (Module 9), some people keep part of a large emergency fund in very low-risk mutual funds; that isn't needed to start.

### Where it should not wait

- **Gold jewellery:** you would need a gold loan or a sale. In a real emergency, a gold loan from a bank is still far better than a loan app (Module 6), but it is a fallback, not the plan.
- **A chitty, shares or crypto:** the value or timing isn't in your control.
- **Money lent to friends and relatives:** it may not come back when you need it.
- **A co-operative society beyond what you can afford to have stuck:** see FIN-M04-L01 and FIN-M09-L07.

### How to build it on a small income

- **Automate:** a standing instruction moves a fixed amount to the emergency account the day after income arrives. Start with any amount: ₹500 a month is ₹6,000 a year.
- **Windfalls:** put at least half of every bonus, gift, DA arrears or big client payment into the fund until it is full.
- **One cut:** use one leak from Module 3 (snacks, subscriptions) and send that amount to the fund.
- **Sell what you don't use:** an old phone, books after an exam, unused items.

### How long will it take?

> **Months to target = (target − saved so far) ÷ monthly saving** (ignoring interest)

The spreadsheet function **NPER** includes interest: `=NPER(rate/12, -monthly, -saved, target)`.

**Worked example:** Anu's full target is ₹54,000; she has ₹6,000 and can save ₹2,500 a month. Without interest: (₹54,000 − ₹6,000) ÷ ₹2,500 = about **20 months**. If she puts half of her exam-season extra income (about ₹2,000 a month for four months a year) in too, it drops to about 16 months.

### Using it and refilling it

When you use the fund for a real emergency, don't feel guilty: that is what it is for. Then pause other goals and refill it first, using the same monthly transfer.

## Local example

**Fathima** set up her emergency fund like this:

| Layer | Amount | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cash at home | ₹3,000 | In a sealed envelope in her cupboard |
| Instant money | ₹20,000 | A savings account at a second bank, no UPI app linked, net banking only |
| Ladder | ₹40,000 so far | Four FDs of ₹10,000 each, maturing every three months |

Her standing instruction moves ₹4,000 on the 2nd of every month, and her rule from FIN-M03-L04 sends anything above three months of business buffer into the fund. When her laptop failed in July, she broke one ₹10,000 FD, paid a small penalty on its interest, and bought a replacement within a day, without touching her credit card.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [DICGC: deposit insurance, what is covered (PDF)](https://website.dicgc.org.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/DICGC_Flyer_0.pdf) | Revise: deposit insurance per bank, to decide how to spread the ladder | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [India Post: saving schemes and current interest rates](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving) | Current deposit rates, if you are considering a post office deposit for part of the fund | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | Finish the safety nets and insurance module if you didn't in FIN-M05-L01 | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Decide your three layers: how much in cash, in instant money and in the ladder, and where each one lives.
2. Choose or open the separate account for instant money (one you don't use for daily spending).
3. Set up a standing instruction for a monthly amount, starting next income day. Any amount counts.
4. Fill in the build-up section of the Emergency tab and calculate the months to your starter and full targets.
5. Make your first transfer today, even ₹100.
6. Write your refill rule: what you pause if you use the fund.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of the standing instruction or first transfer (account numbers covered) and the build-up section of your Emergency tab, saved in 05 Emergency.

## Template: Emergency tab: build-up

```
B10: monthly transfer (₹)
B11: interest rate while saving (e.g. 0.065, or 0)
B12: months to starter  =IF(B6>=B5,0,IF(B11=0,ROUNDUP((B5-B6)/B10,0),ROUNDUP(NPER(B11/12,-B10,-B6,B5),0)))
B13: months to full     =IF(B6>=B4,0,IF(B11=0,ROUNDUP((B4-B6)/B10,0),ROUNDUP(NPER(B11/12,-B10,-B6,B4),0)))
Layers:
Layer,Target (₹),Where,Current (₹)
Cash at home,,,
Instant money,,,
FD ladder,,,
```

## Template: FD ladder planner

```csv
FD,Amount (₹),Opened,Matures,Bank,Rate
1,,,,,
2,,,,,
3,,,,,
4,,,,,
Rule: when one matures and I don't need it, renew it for the longest gap in the ladder.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Keeping the fund in your spending account.** It disappears into daily life. Separate account, no daily card.
- **Locking it all in one long FD.** Use a ladder so you break only what you need.
- **Investing it for higher returns.** Its job is to be there, at full value, on a bad day.
- **Never using it out of guilt, and borrowing instead.** Use it for real emergencies, then refill it.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the main job of an emergency fund?
    - A) To be available, at full value, when a shock hits
    - B) To earn the highest return
    - C) To buy gold
    - D) To save tax
2. Why use an FD ladder for part of the fund?
    - A) It doubles the interest
    - B) You break only one small FD when you need money
    - C) It is required by RBI
    - D) It removes all penalties
3. Target ₹60,000, saved ₹10,000, saving ₹2,500 a month. Ignoring interest, how many months?
    - A) 4
    - B) 25
    - C) 24
    - D) 20
4. Why keep a small amount of cash at home?
    - A) To avoid tax
    - B) Cash earns interest
    - C) For days when the network, UPI or ATMs are down
    - D) Banks require it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Deposit insurance per bank, current deposit rates and the NCFE safety nets module
- **Action:** Set up your emergency fund layers, a monthly standing instruction and your first transfer. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of the standing instruction or first transfer (account numbers covered) and the build-up section of your Emergency tab, saved in 05 Emergency.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** Safety and access matter far more than return here.
2. **B.** Several small FDs with different dates give flexibility.
3. **D.** (60,000 − 10,000) ÷ 2,500 = 20.
4. **C.** During floods and outages, digital payments can stop for days.

sections.title: Module 6: Debt and credit
sections.summary: Understand what borrowing really costs, use credit cards safely, compare loans, read your credit report, and get out of debt with a clear plan, without falling into loan-app traps.
sections.content:
## Overview

Debt can build a life (a sensible education or home loan) or eat one (card balances, flat-rate EMIs, illegal apps). The difference is usually the true cost and whether you can repay from normal income. This module gives you the formulas to see the real cost of any loan, the rules that protect you as a borrower, and a step-by-step way out of debt.

You also download your free credit report and check it for errors and fraud, and you learn how to check any lending app against RBI's public directory. Your Debts tab becomes part of your final plan, even if it shows ₹0 (that is a great result).

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Calculate EMI, total interest and the true yearly rate of any loan, including fees
- Explain how credit card interest works and why paying the minimum is so expensive
- Compare personal, gold, education, home and vehicle loans and read a Key Facts Statement
- Get, read and dispute your credit report
- Plan a debt payoff with the avalanche or snowball method and avoid illegal loan apps

## Time

About 11 hours in total: 9 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 10–12.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M06-L01: How interest works, and good and bad debt (about 2 hours)
2. FIN-M06-L02: Credit cards, EMIs and Buy Now Pay Later (about 2 hours)
3. FIN-M06-L03: Personal, gold, education, home and vehicle loans (about 2 hours)
4. FIN-M06-L04: Credit scores and credit reports (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
5. FIN-M06-L05: Getting out of debt, and loan-app traps (about 2 hours)

## Module project: The true cost of my loans and my debt payoff plan

1. Complete the Debts tab: every debt with EMI, total interest, true rate and verdict (or one real loan offer if you have no debts).
2. Add your payoff order and the month you will be debt-free, with the monthly amount from your budget.
3. Note your credit report check: date, bureau, errors found and disputes.
4. Write your three borrowing rules, for example: "I pay my card in full every month", "I never borrow for wants", "I check every lender in RBI's directory and read the KFS first".
5. Add total debt to your Net Worth tab and debt payments to your Budget tab.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your completed Debts tab with payoff plan and your three borrowing rules, saved in 06 Debt.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| True cost | EMIs only | Interest calculated, fees ignored | EMI, total interest and true rate including fees, for every loan |
| Cards | Not reviewed | Statement read | Payoff simulated and full-payment habit set |
| Loan knowledge | Can't compare | Knows the types | Compared two options for a real need using the KFS |
| Credit report | Not checked | Downloaded | Checked line by line, with disputes raised if needed |
| Payoff plan | None | Order chosen | Monthly plan with a debt-free date, and loan-app rules written |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- List every debt with balance, rate and minimum (FIN-M06-L05, step 1).
- Calculate the true rate of your most expensive debt (FIN-M06-L01).
- Download one free credit report and check it (FIN-M06-L04).
- Write your loan-app rule.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| EMI formula in a spreadsheet | =PMT(annual_rate/12, months, -loan_amount) |
| "12% flat" for 2 years is roughly | About 21.6% a year on a reducing balance. |
| Credit card rule | Pay the total amount due, every month, by the due date. |
| Card closure rule | Within 7 working days if no dues, or ₹500 a day for the delay. |
| Prepayment rule from 2026 | No prepayment charges on individuals' floating-rate loans for non-business purposes sanctioned or renewed from 1 January 2026. |
| Free credit reports | One full report a year from each of the four bureaus, on their own websites. |
| Avalanche vs snowball | Avalanche: highest rate first, saves most. Snowball: smallest balance first, quick wins. |
| Checking a lending app | RBI directory of digital lending apps (Citizen's corner) and the lender named in the KFS. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Thinking "everyone has EMIs, so it's fine".** Common doesn't mean cheap. Calculate the true cost of each one.
- **Ignoring small debts.** BNPL and phone EMIs affect your credit report as much as big loans.
- **Facing debt alone.** Talk to the lender early and tell family; secrecy makes every debt worse.

sections.title: FIN-M06-L01: How interest works, and good and bad debt
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Calculate the EMI, total interest and true yearly cost of any loan, spot a "flat rate" trap, and decide whether a debt is worth taking. **Time:** about 2 hours (30 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 60 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Interest is the price of using someone else's money

- **Simple interest** is charged only on the original amount: ₹10,000 at 10% a year for 2 years = ₹2,000.
- **Compound interest** is charged on the amount plus earlier interest. It makes savings grow (Module 8) and makes unpaid debts grow fast.
- **Reducing-balance interest**, used for most bank loans, is charged each month only on the amount still owed. As you repay, the interest part of each EMI falls and the principal part rises.

### The EMI

An **EMI** (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed monthly payment that clears a loan over its term. The spreadsheet function PMT calculates it:

```
=PMT(annual_rate/12, months, -loan_amount)
```

**Worked example:** a ₹1,00,000 personal loan at 14% a year for 36 months: `=PMT(0.14/12, 36, -100000)` = **₹3,418** a month. Total paid = ₹3,418 × 36 = ₹1,23,039, so the **total interest is ₹23,039**.

### The flat-rate trap

Some shops, finance companies and private lenders quote a **flat rate**: interest on the full amount for the whole term, even though you repay every month. It sounds cheap.

**Worked example:** ₹1,00,000 at "12% flat" for 2 years means interest of ₹24,000, so EMI = ₹1,24,000 ÷ 24 = ₹5,167. The same EMI on a normal reducing-balance loan works out to about **21.6% a year**. Always ask for the reducing-balance rate (often shown as the annual percentage rate, APR), or calculate it:

```
=RATE(24, -5166.67, 100000)*12
```

### The true cost includes fees

Processing fees, documentation charges and bundled insurance are part of the cost. They reduce what you actually receive while the EMI stays the same.

**Worked example:** the ₹1,00,000 loan above, with a ₹2,360 processing fee taken from the amount paid out. You receive ₹97,640 but pay ₹3,418 for 36 months. The true yearly cost is `=RATE(36, -3417.76, 97640)*12` = about **15.7%**, not 14%. A Key Facts Statement from a regulated lender must show the charges; a lender can't charge fees that aren't in it ([Business Standard, July 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/personal-finance/avoiding-fraudulent-loan-apps-rbi-listing-ratings-reviews-key-to-safety-125070900931_1.html)).

### Good debt and bad debt: four questions

There is no perfect rule, but these questions help:

1. **Does it build income or lasting value?** An education loan for a course that leads to a job, or a sensible home loan, can. A loan for a phone, a holiday or a wedding beyond your means doesn't.
2. **Is the true cost reasonable?** 9% for a bank gold loan is very different from 3% a month on a credit card or 1% a day from an illegal app.
3. **Can you repay from normal income, with your emergency fund untouched?** Many planners suggest keeping **all EMIs together below about a third of take-home pay**.
4. **What happens if things go wrong?** Collateral such as gold or a house can be lost; a guarantor's credit is affected too.

Debt for wants that lose value is almost always bad debt. Debt itself is a tool: dangerous when used for the wrong job.

## Local example

A mobile shop in Kuttiady offered **Anu** a ₹24,000 phone on "easy EMI: just ₹2,400 a month for 12 months, 0 down payment". She used the formulas from this lesson:

- Total paid: ₹2,400 × 12 = ₹28,800, so ₹4,800 more than the price.
- True yearly rate: `=RATE(12, -2400, 24000)*12` = about **35%** a year, before a ₹499 "file charge".

She also asked herself the four questions. The phone was an upgrade of a working phone (a want), the cost was high, and the EMI would be 17% of her income in a slow month. She decided to save ₹2,000 a month for the phone instead (a sinking fund) and buy it in a year. "The shop's EMI would have paid for almost two extra months of the phone," she wrote in her log.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Google Docs Editors Help: PMT function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093185) | The PMT function, used for loan EMIs | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 8, "Time Value of Money II: Equal Multiple Payments": read the opening sections on loans and annuities | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Business Standard: how to check a loan app on RBI's list (July 2025)](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/personal-finance/avoiding-fraudulent-loan-apps-rbi-listing-ratings-reviews-key-to-safety-125070900931_1.html) | What a Key Facts Statement is and why fees outside it are not allowed | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Debts** tab and copy the loan true-cost calculator from the template.
2. Enter each loan or EMI you have now: card balances, phone EMIs, gold, education, vehicle or personal loans, and money owed to family. Use the statements for the real rate, term and fees.
3. If you have no loans, enter one real offer instead: a phone EMI, a "no-cost EMI" at checkout or a gold loan quote from a bank.
4. Find the EMI, total interest and true yearly rate of each, including fees.
5. Run the four good-debt questions on each loan and write one line per loan: "good", "acceptable" or "bad", and why.
6. Add up all EMIs and compare with your take-home pay.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Debts tab with EMI, total interest, true rate and a good/acceptable/bad verdict for each loan or offer, saved in 06 Debt.

## Template: loan true-cost calculator

```
Row 1: Loan,Amount borrowed (₹),Annual rate (e.g. 0.14),Months,Fees deducted (₹),EMI (₹),Total paid (₹),Total interest (₹),True yearly rate %,Verdict and why
Row 2:
F2: =PMT(C2/12,D2,-B2)
G2: =F2*D2
H2: =G2-B2
I2: =RATE(D2,-F2,B2-E2)*12*100
Flat-rate check (when a lender quotes a flat rate in C2):
EMI = (B2+B2*C2*D2/12)/D2      true yearly rate % = RATE(D2,-EMI,B2)*12*100
All EMIs as % of take-home: =SUM(F2:F10)/take_home*100
```

## Common mistakes

- **Looking only at the EMI.** A small EMI over a long time can cost far more. Check total interest and the true rate.
- **Believing "flat" or "per month" rates are small.** 12% flat is about 21.6% a year on a reducing balance; 3% a month is 36% a year before compounding.
- **Ignoring fees.** Fees taken from the loan raise the true cost. Use the amount you actually receive.
- **Borrowing for wants because the EMI "fits".** An EMI for a want turns a want into a need for months or years.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which formula gives the EMI of a ₹2,00,000 loan at 12% a year for 24 months?
    - A) =PMT(0.12/12, 24, -200000)
    - B) =200000/24
    - C) =200000*0.12*2
    - D) =PMT(0.12, 24, 200000)
2. A lender quotes "12% flat" for 2 years. Roughly what is the reducing-balance rate?
    - A) 12% a year
    - B) About 21.6% a year
    - C) 24% a year exactly
    - D) 6% a year
3. Why does a processing fee raise the true cost of a loan?
    - A) It lowers the EMI
    - B) It doesn't; fees don't matter
    - C) You receive less money but pay the same EMI
    - D) It is refunded at the end
4. Which is most likely to be bad debt?
    - A) A personal loan for a holiday
    - B) A reasonably priced education loan for a job-oriented course
    - C) A home loan within your means
    - D) None; all debt is the same

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The PMT help page, OpenStax chapter 8's opening sections and the Key Facts Statement explainer
- **Action:** Build a Debts tab with the true cost of every loan you have (or one real loan offer) and a verdict for each. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Debts tab with EMI, total interest, true rate and a good/acceptable/bad verdict for each loan or offer, saved in 06 Debt.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** Monthly rate, number of months, and the loan as a negative present value.
2. **B.** Flat interest is charged on the full amount even as you repay, so the true rate is much higher.
3. **C.** The true rate is calculated on what you actually receive.
4. **A.** It pays for a want that leaves no lasting value, at a high cost.

sections.title: FIN-M06-L02: Credit cards, EMIs and Buy Now Pay Later
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Read a credit card statement, see why paying only the minimum is so expensive, check "no-cost EMI" offers, and use your rights under RBI's card rules. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 65 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A credit card is a short loan every month. Used well, it is free: you pay the full bill by the due date and pay no interest. Used badly, it is one of the most expensive debts in India.

### How a card bill works

- **Statement date:** the bill is made, listing everything spent in the billing cycle.
- **Due date:** usually a few weeks later. Pay the **total amount due** by this date and you pay no interest.
- **Minimum amount due:** a small part of the bill. Paying it avoids a late fee, but interest is charged on the rest, at a high monthly rate written in your card's terms (look for "finance charges" in the Most Important Terms and Conditions, or MITC).
- **Lost interest-free period:** if any part of the last bill is unpaid, new purchases also start paying interest from the day you buy.

### RBI rules that protect you

RBI's card rules, as amended in March 2024 ([RBI](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/FS_Notification.aspx?Id=12620), check current rules), include:

- The statement must warn that paying only the minimum due stretches repayment and raises interest.
- **Late payment charges** apply only to the amount still unpaid after the due date, and interest only to what is outstanding after payments and refunds.
- You can **change your billing cycle** at least once.
- If you ask to **close your card** and have no dues, the issuer must close it within 7 working days or pay you ₹500 for every day of delay.
- No card can be issued or upgraded **without your consent**.

### The minimum-due trap, in numbers

**Worked example** (made-up but typical): a ₹50,000 balance at 3.5% a month, with no new spending.

| How you repay | Months to clear | Total interest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only the minimum: 5% of the balance (at least ₹500) | 142 months (about 11 years) | ₹1,00,832 |
| A fixed ₹5,000 every month | 13 months | ₹12,633 |

Paying the minimum, you would pay **more in interest than you borrowed**, and take about 11 years. The rule: **pay the full bill every month**. If you can't, the card balance is your first debt to attack (FIN-M06-L05), and the card goes in a drawer until it is cleared.

### "No-cost EMI"

A "no-cost EMI" usually means the interest is hidden: the seller gives the lender a discount you would otherwise have got, or you pay a processing fee. Before choosing it, compare: (a) the price if you pay in full, (b) the total of all EMIs plus fees. If (b) is higher, it isn't no-cost.

### Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) and small app credit

BNPL lets you pay later or in parts for online shopping. It is still a loan: missed payments bring late fees and are reported to credit bureaus, hurting your credit score (FIN-M06-L04). Many BNPL purchases are small wants, exactly the spending Module 1 asked you to choose carefully.

### Using a card well

Use one card, set up auto-pay for the **full amount**, keep spending far below the limit, and treat the card as a payment tool, not extra money. If you can't trust yourself with it yet, don't get one; a debit card and UPI do almost everything.

## Local example

**Rahul** got a credit card six months into his job. By month five, his statement showed ₹38,000: a phone accessory, flight tickets for a friend's wedding in Bengaluru, and many small restaurant bills. He paid the minimum twice "because salary was tight that month".

In his third statement he saw finance charges of ₹1,200 and new purchases were charging interest from day one. He read the MITC, found the monthly rate, and put his balance into the payoff simulator from this lesson: paying ₹4,000 a month would clear it in about 12 months; ₹6,500 a month in about 7, with about ₹3,700 less interest.

He chose ₹6,500, took the card off his phone's payment apps, and set auto-pay to "total amount due" for after it was cleared. He kept the card: closing it wasn't necessary once he trusted himself again.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [RBI: credit and debit card rules, amendment of March 2024](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/FS_Notification.aspx?Id=12620) | The March 2024 amendment: minimum-due warning, late charges, billing cycle, closure in 7 working days and consent rules | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The e-LMS module on money and transactions: the part on cards and credit | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. If you have a credit card, open your latest statement and the MITC. Find: statement date, due date, total due, minimum due, monthly interest rate and late fee. Write them down.
2. Copy the card payoff simulator into your Debts tab and enter your balance and rate (if you have no card, use the ₹50,000 example).
3. Compare paying the minimum with a fixed amount you can afford.
4. Check one "no-cost EMI" offer on a shopping site or in a shop: price paid in full vs total of EMIs plus fees.
5. If you have a card: set auto-pay to the total amount due, or write down the date you will pay in full each month.

**Proof to record:** Your filled-in statement facts (card number covered), the simulator result comparing minimum and fixed payments, and your no-cost EMI comparison, saved in 06 Debt.

## Template: card payoff simulator (one row per month)

```
B1: monthly interest rate (e.g. 0.035)    D1: minimum due % (e.g. 0.05)    F1: minimum amount (e.g. 500)    H1: fixed payment (0 to use minimum)
Row 3 headings: Month,Opening balance,Interest,Payment,Closing balance
Row 4: A4: 1   B4: (your balance)
C4: =B4*$B$1
D4: =MIN(IF($H$1>0,$H$1,MAX(B4*$D$1,$F$1)),B4+C4)
E4: =B4+C4-D4
Row 5: A5: =A4+1   B5: =E4   then copy C4:E4 down to row 5
Copy row 5 down until the closing balance reaches 0.
Total interest: =SUM(C4:C200)     Months: =COUNTIF(B4:B200,">0.5")
```

## Template: no-cost EMI check

```
Price if paid in full today (after any discount): ₹____
EMI ₹____ × ____ months = ₹____
Processing fee and other charges: ₹____
Total through EMI: ₹____
Is the EMI total higher than the full price? Yes / No  →  if yes, it is not "no-cost"
```

## Common mistakes

- **Paying only the minimum due.** It keeps the card active but the debt alive for years. Pay the total amount due.
- **Treating the credit limit as money you have.** The limit is the bank's risk appetite, not your budget.
- **Missing that new purchases charge interest after a partial payment.** Once a bill is partly unpaid, the interest-free period is lost until you clear it.
- **Collecting cards.** One card used well is enough. More cards mean more fees and more temptation.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What should you pay each month to avoid card interest?
    - A) Half the bill
    - B) The minimum amount due
    - C) The total amount due, by the due date
    - D) Nothing until the next bill
2. Under RBI's rules, how fast must an issuer close a card with no dues after you ask?
    - A) Whenever it likes
    - B) Only after a year
    - C) Within 7 working days, or pay ₹500 a day for the delay
    - D) Within 90 days
3. In the course example, how does paying only the minimum compare with a fixed ₹5,000 a month?
    - A) Cheaper in total
    - B) Years longer and many times more interest
    - C) About the same
    - D) Faster
4. When is a "no-cost EMI" not really no-cost?
    - A) When the shop is in Kerala
    - B) When the EMIs plus fees add up to more than the full price
    - C) When you pay by UPI
    - D) Never

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** RBI's March 2024 card rules and the NCFE section on cards and credit
- **Action:** Read your card statement (or the example), run the payoff simulator and check one no-cost EMI offer. It is done when your proof is saved: your filled-in statement facts (card number covered), the simulator result comparing minimum and fixed payments, and your no-cost EMI comparison, saved in 06 Debt.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Only paying the full bill keeps the card interest-free.
2. **C.** The rule includes a ₹500-a-day penalty for delays.
3. **B.** The minimum shrinks as the balance shrinks, so repayment drags on for years.
4. **B.** Hidden interest shows up as a lost discount or a fee.

sections.title: FIN-M06-L03: Personal, gold, education, home and vehicle loans
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare the main loan types in India on cost, risk and rules, read a Key Facts Statement, and know your rights on prepayment, gold loans and education loans. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 65 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The main loans, side by side

| Loan | Usually for | Security | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Personal loan | Anything; often wants | None (unsecured), so rates are higher | True rate with fees; avoid for wants |
| Gold loan | Short-term needs; emergencies | Your gold jewellery | Loan-to-value, interest method, renewal and auction rules |
| Education loan | Course fees and costs | Sometimes none, under government schemes | Moratorium, interest during study, subsidy eligibility |
| Home loan | Buying or building a house | The house | Floating vs fixed rate, tenure, prepayment, the builder's RERA registration |
| Vehicle loan | Two-wheeler or car | The vehicle | Total cost; the vehicle loses value every year |

### Read the Key Facts Statement (KFS)

Before signing, ask for the **Key Facts Statement**: a short summary with the annual percentage rate (APR), all fees, the EMI schedule and penalties. For loans through apps, the KFS also names the actual regulated lender, and the lender can't charge fees that aren't in it ([Business Standard, July 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/personal-finance/avoiding-fraudulent-loan-apps-rbi-listing-ratings-reviews-key-to-safety-125070900931_1.html)). If a lender won't give you a KFS, walk away.

### Gold loans

Gold loans are common in Kerala and can be a sensible short-term fallback, far better than app loans. Key points:

- **Loan-to-value (LTV):** the loan as a share of the gold's value. RBI raised the LTV limit to **85% for small gold loans up to ₹2.5 lakh** in June 2025 ([Business Standard headline](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/gold-loan-ltv-raised-to-85-percent-up-to-rs-2-5-lakh-rbi-125060601173_1.html), check current rules). A higher LTV means more cash now and less cushion if gold prices fall.
- **How interest is paid:** monthly, or all at the end. With "bullet" repayment, interest builds up; know the total before you sign.
- **If you don't repay,** the lender can auction your gold after notices. Keep the renewal and closing dates in your calendar.
- Compare banks, NBFCs and co-operative banks on the rate, valuation, charges and auction rules.

### Education loans and PM-Vidyalaxmi

Under **PM-Vidyalaxmi**, approved in November 2024, students admitted to quality higher education institutions (based on NIRF rankings: the top 100 overall, by category or by domain, state government institutions ranked 101 to 200, and all central government institutions) can get **collateral-free, guarantor-free education loans** through a unified "PM-Vidyalaxmi" portal. The government gives a 75% credit guarantee on loans up to ₹7.5 lakh, and students with family income up to ₹8 lakh who aren't covered by other schemes get **3% interest subvention during the moratorium on loans up to ₹10 lakh** ([PIB, November 2024](https://education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/PIB2071134.pdf), check current rules).

In most education loans, interest builds up during the course and the moratorium, then EMIs start. Calculate the EMI on the full amount you will owe when repayment starts, and compare it with the starting salary of the job the course leads to.

### Home loans and prepayment

- **Floating rate:** changes with the lender's benchmark. Many floating loans are linked to an external benchmark such as RBI's repo rate, which RBI raised from 5.25% to 5.50% in October 2026 ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/)); when it rises, your EMI or tenure can rise too.
- **Prepayment:** under RBI's directions, lenders can't charge **prepayment penalties on floating-rate loans to individuals for non-business purposes** sanctioned or renewed from 1 January 2026, whether you prepay part or all ([Angel One](https://www.angelone.in/news/personal-finance/rbi-new-rule-no-prepayment-penalty-on-floating-loans-from-jan-1-2026), check current rules). Prepaying even small amounts early in a home loan saves a lot of interest.

**Worked example:** a ₹20 lakh home loan for 20 years at 8.5% has an EMI of ₹17,356. If the rate rises to 8.75%, the EMI rises by about ₹318 a month, or the lender extends the tenure instead.

FIN-M11-L02 covers whether to buy a house at all.

### Vehicle loans

A vehicle loses value from the day you buy it, and the loan adds interest on top. Prefer a bigger down payment and a shorter loan; include insurance, fuel and maintenance in the monthly cost (FIN-M11-L01).

## Local example

**Rahul's** younger sister got admission to a nursing course, and the family needed ₹1,60,000 for the first year. His mother suggested a gold loan on 3 pavan (24 grams). The jeweller's valuation was ₹2,16,000 (made-up rate).

Rahul compared two options with the KFS of each:

|  | Gold loan from a bank | Education loan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amount | ₹1,60,000 (about 74% of the gold's value) | ₹1,60,000 for year 1, more for later years |
| Repayment starts | Interest monthly; principal within the loan term | After the course and moratorium |
| Risk | The gold can be auctioned if unpaid | Debt in his sister's name, Rahul as co-borrower |
| Subsidy | None | Check: does the college qualify under PM-Vidyalaxmi, and is the family income within the limit? |

They found the college wasn't on the PM-Vidyalaxmi list, but a bank education loan was still possible with Rahul as co-borrower. They chose the education loan for the course and kept the gold, because a gold loan for a four-year course would have meant renewing and worrying for four years. Rahul added the expected EMI to his Debts tab under "starts in 2030".

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [PIB: PM-Vidyalaxmi education loan scheme approved (PDF, November 2024)](https://education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/PIB2071134.pdf) | PM-Vidyalaxmi: eligibility, guarantee and interest subvention | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Angel One: no prepayment charges on floating-rate loans from 1 January 2026](https://www.angelone.in/news/personal-finance/rbi-new-rule-no-prepayment-penalty-on-floating-loans-from-jan-1-2026) | Prepayment charges: which loans, from when | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Business Standard: gold loan LTV raised to 85% for loans up to ₹2.5 lakh (June 2025)](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/gold-loan-ltv-raised-to-85-percent-up-to-rs-2-5-lakh-rbi-125060601173_1.html) | Gold loan LTV change (headline) | 2 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 (headline checked) |
| [SCC Online: RBI raises the repo rate to 5.50% (October 2026)](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/) | The October 2026 repo rate decision | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Business Standard: how to check a loan app on RBI's list (July 2025)](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/finance/personal-finance/avoiding-fraudulent-loan-apps-rbi-listing-ratings-reviews-key-to-safety-125070900931_1.html) | The Key Facts Statement and checking an app lender | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. For every loan in your Debts tab, find the KFS or sanction letter and note: type (floating or fixed), APR, prepayment rules and what happens if you miss a payment.
2. If you have a floating-rate loan, check whether its rate has changed after the October 2026 repo rate decision.
3. Fill in the loan comparison template for one real decision: two ways to borrow for the same need (for example a bank gold loan vs a personal loan), or two lenders for the same loan.
4. If education may be in your family's plans, check whether the institutions you are considering qualify under PM-Vidyalaxmi, using the official portal named in the PIB release.
5. Write a rule for gold loans: when you would use one, and which dates go in your calendar.

**Proof to record:** Your loan comparison with KFS details for both options and your gold-loan rule, saved in 06 Debt.

## Template: loan comparison

```csv
Need: ____  Amount: ₹____
,Option A,Option B
Lender (regulated? name on KFS),,
Type (personal / gold / education / home / vehicle),,
APR from the KFS,,
Fees (₹),,
EMI (₹) =PMT(rate/12,months,-amount),,
Total interest (₹),,
Prepayment rules,,
Security (gold / house / vehicle / none),,
What happens if I miss a payment,,
Decision and why:
```

## Common mistakes

- **Signing without a KFS.** The KFS is your one-page truth. No KFS, no loan.
- **Forgetting gold loan dates.** Missed renewals can lead to auction notices. Put dates in your calendar.
- **Ignoring interest during an education loan's moratorium.** Interest usually builds up during the course; plan the EMI on the full amount.
- **Never prepaying.** On floating-rate personal (non-business) loans from 2026 there is no prepayment penalty; small prepayments save a lot.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did RBI change for small gold loans in June 2025, per the course's source?
    - A) Gold loans were banned
    - B) LTV up to 85% for loans up to ₹2.5 lakh
    - C) LTV cut to 50%
    - D) No interest on gold loans
2. Under PM-Vidyalaxmi, who gets 3% interest subvention?
    - A) Everyone, on any loan
    - B) Only government employees
    - C) Students with family income up to ₹8 lakh, on loans up to ₹10 lakh, during the moratorium
    - D) Only students abroad
3. You have a floating-rate home loan sanctioned in 2026 for your own house. Can the bank charge a penalty if you prepay part of it?
    - A) Yes, always 2%
    - B) Only in the first year
    - C) Only if you prepay in cash
    - D) No, under RBI's directions for individuals' non-business floating loans
4. What is a Key Facts Statement?
    - A) A short summary of a loan's APR, fees, schedule and penalties
    - B) Your credit report
    - C) A gold valuation certificate
    - D) An income tax form

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** PM-Vidyalaxmi, the prepayment rules, the gold loan LTV change, the repo rate decision and the KFS explainer
- **Action:** Note KFS details for your loans and compare two ways to borrow for one real need. It is done when your proof is saved: your loan comparison with KFS details for both options and your gold-loan rule, saved in 06 Debt.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** The headline reports an 85% LTV for small gold loans up to ₹2.5 lakh.
2. **C.** Those are the conditions in the PIB release (check current rules).
3. **D.** Prepayment charges are not allowed on such loans sanctioned or renewed from 1 January 2026.
4. **A.** It lets you compare loans on one page, and fees outside it can't be charged.
