sections.title: FIN-M08-L01: Inflation and compounding: the two forces on your money
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Calculate real returns, the future value of a lump sum and a SIP, and what a future amount is worth in today's rupees, in a Calculators tab. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Two forces act on every rupee you save: **inflation** quietly shrinks what it can buy, and **compounding** can make it grow. Investing is the art of making compounding beat inflation without taking risks you can't handle.

### Inflation

Inflation is the general rise in prices, measured in India mainly by the **consumer price index (CPI)**. The official target is **4%, within a band of 2% to 6%**, until March 2031 ([Outlook Money, March 2026](https://www.outlookmoney.com/banking/rbi-to-maintain-4-per-cent-inflation-target-until-2031-centre)). CPI inflation was **4.8% in August 2026**, and RBI raised its policy repo rate to 5.50% in October 2026 to keep prices in check ([SCC Online, October 2026](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/)).

At 5% inflation, something that costs ₹1,000 today costs about ₹1,629 in 10 years. Put the other way, **₹10,00,000 received 20 years from now buys only what about ₹3,76,889 buys today**:

> **Today's value of a future amount = future amount ÷ (1 + inflation) ^ years**

### Real return

The return that matters is what you earn **after** inflation:

> **Real return ≈ return − inflation** (exactly: (1 + return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1)

- Savings account at 3%, inflation at 5%: real return about **−1.9%**. The balance grows; its buying power shrinks.
- A deposit at 7%, inflation at 5%: real return about **+1.9%**, before tax on the interest.

Money for the next few years should be safe even if its real return is small. Money for 10 or 20 years needs a positive real return, or your goals keep running away from you.

### Compounding

Compounding means earning returns on your earlier returns:

> **Future value = amount today × (1 + yearly return) ^ years**

₹1,00,000 at 8% a year grows to about ₹2,15,892 in 10 years, ₹4,66,096 in 20 years and ₹10,06,266 in 30 years. The last 10 years add more than the first 20, because the base is bigger. **Time is the most powerful part of the formula.**

The **rule of 72** is a quick check: money doubles in about **72 ÷ return** years. At 8%, about 9 years; at 6%, about 12; at 12%, about 6.

### A SIP: investing every month

A **systematic investment plan (SIP)** puts in a fixed amount every month. The spreadsheet FV function gives the future value:

```
=FV(0.08/12, 33*12, -2000, 0, 1)
```

**Worked example:** starting at 27, ₹2,000 a month at an assumed 8% a year until 60 (33 years) grows to about **₹38,93,073**, from ₹7,92,000 paid in. Starting at 37 (23 years), it grows to only about **₹15,87,979**, from ₹5,52,000. To catch up, the late starter would need ₹4,000 a month, and would still end with about ₹31,75,957.

### A warning about assumed returns

Every number above uses an **assumed** return. Real investments don't grow at a steady 8%: some years they fall, some years they jump, and the average over your period is unknown in advance. Use calculators to understand the effect of time and amounts, not to promise yourself a result. When anyone shows you a calculator with a high return to sell you something, ask what happens in a bad decade (FIN-M08-L02).

## Local example

**Anu**, 27, and her friend **Sreeja**, 37, compared notes after a PSC class. Sreeja had saved nothing for retirement: "I'll start when I have a government job, with a bigger amount."

Anu put both of them into her new Calculators tab, at an assumed 8%: ₹2,000 a month from Anu's age until 60 gave about ₹38,93,073; the same amount from Sreeja's age gave about ₹15,87,979. Sreeja would need to put in twice as much each month just to come close.

Then they did the inflation step: at 5% inflation, Anu's ₹38,93,073 in 33 years would buy what about ₹7,78,118 buys today. "So the big number isn't as big as it looks," Sreeja said. "But starting late makes it much smaller." She started a small recurring deposit that week, planning to move it to a proper retirement plan after Module 12.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 3, "Economic Foundations: Money and Rates" (inflation and interest) and chapter 7 (future value): read the sections on inflation and compounding | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Outlook Money: the 4% inflation target continues until 2031 (March 2026)](https://www.outlookmoney.com/banking/rbi-to-maintain-4-per-cent-inflation-target-until-2031-centre) | India's inflation target until 2031 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SCC Online: RBI raises the repo rate to 5.50% (October 2026)](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/) | The October 2026 policy decision: repo rate and recent CPI inflation | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Calculators** tab with the template: lump-sum future value, SIP future value, today's value of a future amount, real return and the rule of 72.
2. Test each calculator with the worked examples from this lesson and check you get the same answers.
3. Calculate the real return on your own savings account and on one FD rate from Module 4, using 5% inflation.
4. Put your own numbers into the SIP calculator: the monthly amount you could invest, and the years until a long-term goal. Then try starting 5 years later.
5. Write two sentences: what surprised you, and what you will do differently.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your working Calculators tab with your own numbers and your two sentences, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: Calculators tab (labels in column A, inputs in B)

```
LUMP SUM
B2: amount today (₹)   B3: yearly return (e.g. 0.08)   B4: years
B5: future value   =B2*(1+B3)^B4

SIP (monthly, invested at the start of each month)
B8: monthly amount (₹)   B9: yearly return   B10: years
B11: future value  =FV(B9/12,B10*12,-B8,0,1)
B12: total paid    =B8*B10*12
B13: growth        =B11-B12

TODAY'S VALUE OF A FUTURE AMOUNT
B16: future amount (₹)   B17: inflation (e.g. 0.05)   B18: years
B19: in today's rupees  =B16/(1+B17)^B18

REAL RETURN
B22: return (e.g. 0.07)   B23: inflation (e.g. 0.05)
B24: real return %  =((1+B22)/(1+B23)-1)*100

RULE OF 72
B27: yearly return in % (e.g. 8)
B28: years to double, about  =72/B27
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring inflation.** A goal 20 years away needs future rupees. Always convert both ways: future cost, and today's value of a future amount.
- **Treating an assumed return as a promise.** Calculators show the effect of time and amounts. Real returns vary year to year.
- **Waiting for a bigger income to start.** Time does more work than amount. Start small now and raise the amount later.
- **Keeping long-term money in a savings account.** A negative real return slowly eats it. Long-term money needs growth (FIN-M08-L03).

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. A deposit pays 7% and inflation is 5%. What is the real return, roughly?
    - A) −2%
    - B) 7%
    - C) About 2%
    - D) 12%
2. By the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
    - A) About 3 years
    - B) About 12 years
    - C) About 72 years
    - D) About 6 years
3. Which formula gives the future value of ₹2,000 a month for 20 years at 8%, invested at the start of each month?
    - A) =PMT(0.08, 20, 2000)
    - B) =2000*20*12
    - C) =FV(0.08/12, 20*12, -2000, 0, 1)
    - D) =2000*(1+0.08)^20
4. What is India's CPI inflation target for 2026 to 2031?
    - A) 4%, with a band of 2% to 6%
    - B) 0%
    - C) 10% to 12%
    - D) 8%
5. Why does starting 10 years earlier make such a big difference?
    - A) Inflation is lower for young people
    - B) Banks pay more to young people
    - C) Compounding has more years to work, and the last years add the most
    - D) It doesn't make a difference

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapters 3 and 7 on inflation and compounding, the inflation target and the October 2026 policy decision
- **Action:** Build a Calculators tab, test it, and run your own numbers for real return and a SIP. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your working Calculators tab with your own numbers and your two sentences, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Real return ≈ 7% − 5%; exactly (1.07 ÷ 1.05) − 1 ≈ 1.9%.
2. **B.** 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
3. **C.** FV with a monthly rate, the number of months, the payment and type 1.
4. **A.** The target was kept at 4% ± 2% until March 2031.
5. **C.** Time is the exponent in the compounding formula.

sections.title: FIN-M08-L02: Risk, return and the main asset classes
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain the main kinds of investment risk, describe each asset class honestly, and score your own risk profile. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Risk is more than "losing money"

| Risk | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market risk | Prices go up and down, sometimes a lot | Share prices fall sharply in a bad year |
| Inflation risk | Returns don't keep up with prices | A savings account at 3% when prices rise 5% |
| Credit (default) risk | The borrower doesn't pay you back | A company or society fails to repay a deposit or bond |
| Interest-rate risk | Bond and debt fund prices fall when rates rise | A long-term bond fund dips after a rate rise |
| Liquidity risk | You can't sell quickly at a fair price | Land that takes a year to sell |
| Concentration risk | Too much in one thing | All savings in one stock, one plot or one society |
| Fraud risk | The product or the seller is a scam | A "scheme" promising 5% a month (Module 15) |

There is no investment without risk; even "safe" deposits carry inflation risk.

### The main asset classes

| Asset class | Examples | Return potential | Main risks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cash and deposits | Savings, FDs, RDs | Low; may not beat inflation after tax | Inflation; credit risk above insurance limits |
| Debt (lending) | Government small savings, PPF, EPF, bonds, debt mutual funds | Low to moderate | Interest-rate and credit risk; government-backed schemes have very low credit risk |
| Equity (ownership) | Shares, equity mutual funds, index funds | Highest over long periods | Large falls in bad years; years to recover |
| Gold | Gold ETFs, gold mutual funds, jewellery | Varies; often rises when other assets fall | Long flat periods; jewellery has making charges and purity issues |
| Real estate | Land, a house, REITs | Varies by place | Illiquid, large amounts, legal issues, costs |
| Speculative | Crypto, derivatives (F&O) | Uncertain | Very high volatility; SEBI found about 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in 2024-25 ([Moneylife](https://moneylife.in/article/91-percentage-of-retail-traders-lost-money-in-derivatives-losses-in-fo-surged-41-percentage-to-rs105-lakh-crore-in-fy2425-sebi-study/77613.html)) |

### The risk–return trade-off

Higher possible returns come with higher risk. It never works the other way: **"high returns with no risk" doesn't exist**. When someone offers it, you are looking at a misunderstanding or a fraud.

Equity's long-term return potential is higher because investors are paid for living through its falls. If you will panic and sell in a fall, you get the falls without the long-term reward.

### The riskometer

Every mutual fund in India shows a **riskometer**, SEBI's standard risk scale with six levels: **Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High** ([AMFI](https://www.mutualfundssahihai.com/en/what-riskometer-and-what-are-different-levels)). It is based on the fund's holdings, volatility, and credit and interest-rate risk, and must appear in factsheets and promotional material ([SEBI investor site](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html)). You will use it to compare funds in FIN-M09-L02.

### Your risk profile: two different things

- **Risk capacity:** how much loss your finances can survive. A full emergency fund, stable income, insurance, no expensive debt and a long time horizon all raise it.
- **Risk tolerance:** how much loss you can live with emotionally without panicking.

Invest according to the **lower** of the two. A government employee with a pension may have high capacity but low tolerance; a young freelancer may feel brave but have low capacity.

### Time horizon changes everything

Money needed in 2 years can't wait for a market to recover; money needed in 20 years can. So the same person can have safe money for short goals and growth money for long ones. That is the idea behind asset allocation, in the next lesson.

## Local example

**Fathima** scored herself with the risk profile in this lesson. Her **tolerance** came out high: she enjoys reading about markets and wasn't worried by the idea of a 30% fall. But her **capacity** came out low: irregular income, an emergency fund only half built, and a two-wheeler loan.

Her conclusion: "My head says high risk, my situation says not yet." She decided that until her emergency fund was full and her loan cleared, new long-term money would go mostly to safer options, with only a small share in equity, rising once her capacity improved. She wrote the rule in her Calculators tab so she wouldn't change her mind after a good month in the markets.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AMFI (Mutual Funds Sahi Hai): the six riskometer levels](https://www.mutualfundssahihai.com/en/what-riskometer-and-what-are-different-levels) | The six riskometer levels | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SEBI investor website: riskometer](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html) | How the riskometer is decided and where you will see it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Moneylife: SEBI study, 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in 2024-25](https://moneylife.in/article/91-percentage-of-retail-traders-lost-money-in-derivatives-losses-in-fo-surged-41-percentage-to-rs105-lakh-crore-in-fy2425-sebi-study/77613.html) | SEBI's study of losses in futures and options trading | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 15, "How to Think about Investing": read the opening sections on risk and return | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Answer the 10 risk-profile questions honestly and add up your capacity and tolerance scores.
2. Write your profile: the lower of the two scores decides it.
3. In your Goals tab, add a column "time horizon" and mark each goal short (under 3 years), medium (3 to 7) or long (over 7).
4. For each risk in the table, write one place it already exists in your family's money (for example, concentration: all savings in one co-op society).
5. Write one rule that follows from your profile, like Fathima's.

**Proof to record:** Your scored risk profile, the horizon column in your Goals tab and your one rule, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: risk profile (score each answer 1 to 3)

```
CAPACITY (what your finances can survive)
1. Emergency fund: none (1) / partly built (2) / full (3)
2. Income: irregular (1) / steady private job (2) / permanent or very secure (3)
3. Expensive debt (cards, personal loans): yes (1) / some (2) / none (3)
4. Health and life cover in place: no (1) / partly (2) / yes (3)
5. Years until you need this money: under 3 (1) / 3 to 7 (2) / over 7 (3)
Capacity score: ____ / 15

TOLERANCE (what you can live with)
6. If your investment fell 25% in a year, you would: sell everything (1) / wait, worried (2) / hold or add more (3)
7. You prefer: certain small growth (1) / some ups and downs (2) / big ups and downs for more growth (3)
8. You check investments: daily and worry (1) / monthly (2) / a few times a year (3)
9. Past loss experience: panicked (1) / no experience (2) / stayed calm (3)
10. Sleep test: losses would keep you awake (1) / sometimes (2) / no (3)
Tolerance score: ____ / 15

Profile = the LOWER score:  5-8 cautious   9-11 balanced   12-15 growth
```

## Common mistakes

- **Thinking deposits are risk-free.** They carry inflation risk, and credit risk above insurance limits or in unlicensed societies.
- **Judging risk by last year's returns.** A great year says nothing about the next one. Look at what can go wrong.
- **Investing by tolerance alone.** Courage doesn't pay bills in a crisis. Capacity decides too.
- **Believing "guaranteed high returns".** High return and no risk never come together. It is the first sign of a scam.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which risk does a savings account carry even though the balance never falls?
    - A) Market risk
    - B) Inflation risk
    - C) Liquidity risk
    - D) No risk at all
2. How many levels does SEBI's riskometer have?
    - A) Two
    - B) Three
    - C) Ten
    - D) Six
3. Your tolerance score is high but your capacity is low. What should decide your investments?
    - A) The higher one: tolerance
    - B) Last year's best fund
    - C) Whatever friends do
    - D) The lower one: capacity
4. What did SEBI's study find about individual F&O traders in 2024-25?
    - A) Most made steady profits
    - B) Half doubled their money
    - C) Nobody traded
    - D) About 91% lost money

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The riskometer (AMFI and SEBI), SEBI's F&O loss study and OpenStax chapter 15's opening sections
- **Action:** Score your risk profile, mark each goal's time horizon and write one rule. It is done when your proof is saved: your scored risk profile, the horizon column in your Goals tab and your one rule, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** If interest is below inflation, buying power shrinks.
2. **D.** Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High, Very High.
3. **D.** Invest by the lower of the two so a bad year doesn't break your plan.
4. **D.** Net losses were over ₹1 lakh crore in the year.

sections.title: FIN-M08-L03: Asset allocation, diversification and rebalancing
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Set a target asset allocation for your long-term money based on your goals and risk profile, and use a formula to know when to rebalance. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Asset allocation

**Asset allocation** is how you split your investments between asset classes: equity, debt, gold and cash. It matters more for your long-term result than which individual fund or stock you pick, because it decides how much your money can grow and how far it can fall.

### Allocation by goal

The simplest method follows the time horizons you marked in FIN-M08-L02:

| Goal horizon | Typical allocation | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 3 years | All safe: deposits, RDs, small savings, very low-risk debt | No time to recover from a fall |
| 3 to 7 years | Mostly safe, some equity (for example 20–40%) | Some growth, limited damage in a bad year |
| Over 7 years (retirement, a child's education) | More equity (for example 50–70%), the rest debt, perhaps some gold | Time to ride out falls; needs to beat inflation |

These are examples to think with, not recommendations. Adjust them for your risk profile: a cautious profile uses the lower equity numbers or less. One rule of thumb some people use for long-term money is "100 minus your age" in equity; treat it as a starting point for thinking, not an answer.

Remember money you already have in **EPF, GPF or PPF**: it is debt. If you are a government employee with GPF or NPS contributions (Module 14), count them in your allocation.

### Diversification

**Don't put all your eggs in one basket**, within and across asset classes:

- **Across classes:** equity, debt and gold rarely all fall at the same time.
- **Within a class:** one company's shares can go to zero; an index fund holding many companies is far less likely to. One co-operative society can fail; deposits spread across insured banks and government schemes are safer.
- **Kerala's common concentration:** most family wealth in one plot of land, one house and gold. Diversifying doesn't mean selling the house; it means new savings go elsewhere.

### Rebalancing

Over time, the assets that grew fastest become a bigger share than you planned. If equity rises, your portfolio becomes riskier without you deciding it. **Rebalancing** brings it back to target:

1. **Check once a year**, on a fixed date (your yearly review, FIN-M17-L03).
2. **Rebalance if any class has drifted more than 5 percentage points** from its target (your rule; some use 10).
3. **First, direct new money** to the asset class that is below target. This avoids selling.
4. **Only if needed, sell** some of what is above target and buy what is below, thinking about tax (Module 10) and exit loads.

**Worked example:** Rahul's target is 60% equity, 35% debt, 5% gold. After a strong year his ₹2,00,000 long-term money is ₹1,36,000 equity (68%), ₹56,000 debt (28%) and ₹8,000 gold (4%). Equity has drifted 8 points over. He sends his next six months of new investments entirely to debt, which brings him back near target without selling.

Rebalancing feels wrong: it means adding to what has done badly and slowing what has done well. That is exactly why it works: it makes you buy low and sell high by rule, not by feeling.

## Local example

**Anu** set her first allocation. Her short goals (emergency fund, course fees, two-wheeler) stay 100% safe in her savings account, RD and FDs. Her only long goal is retirement, starting small after Module 12.

For the retirement money, her risk profile came out **balanced**, so she wrote a target of **50% equity (through index funds, once she has studied them in Module 9), 45% debt (PPF), 5% gold**. Her rule: rebalance on 1 April each year if anything drifts more than 5 points, by sending new money to the lagging class first.

She noticed her family's wealth was mostly land and gold jewellery. She didn't try to change her parents' choices; she wrote, "My own new savings go to what our family doesn't have yet: insured deposits, PPF and, later, diversified equity."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 15, "How to Think about Investing": the sections on diversification and portfolios | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The long-term planning module (revision) with allocation in mind | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. In your Goals tab, add the target allocation for each goal's money using its horizon and your profile.
2. Make an **Allocation** tab with the template: list what you already hold (deposits, PPF, EPF, gold, any funds or shares), with asset class and value.
3. Enter your target percentages for long-term money and let the formulas show actual percentages and drift.
4. Write your rebalancing rule: date, drift limit, and "new money first".
5. Write one sentence on your biggest concentration risk and what you will do about it with new savings.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Allocation tab with targets, actuals and the drift formula, and your rebalancing rule, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: Allocation tab

```
Holdings (rows 2-30): Holding,Asset class (Equity/Debt/Gold/Cash),Value (₹),For which goal
Summary (columns F-J):
F2: Equity   F3: Debt   F4: Gold   F5: Cash
G: actual value   G2: =SUMIF($B$2:$B$30,F2,$C$2:$C$30)   (copy to G3:G5)
H: actual %       H2: =IF(SUM($G$2:$G$5)>0,G2/SUM($G$2:$G$5)*100,0)
I: target %       (type: e.g. 60, 35, 5, 0)
J: drift          J2: =H2-I2
K: action         K2: =IF(ABS(J2)>5,IF(J2>0,"Over: send new money elsewhere","Under: send new money here"),"OK")
```

## Template: my rebalancing rule

```
I check my allocation every year on ____ (date).
If any asset class is more than ___ percentage points away from target, I rebalance.
First I send new money to the class below target. I sell only if that isn't enough, after checking tax and exit loads.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing funds before choosing an allocation.** Decide the split first; picking products comes after (Module 9).
- **Forgetting EPF, GPF and PPF.** They are debt. Count them, or you may hold more debt than you think.
- **Rebalancing too often.** Once a year with a drift limit is enough; frequent changes add costs and taxes.
- **Mistaking many products for diversification.** Five funds that hold the same companies aren't diversified. Look at what they own.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Money for a goal in 2 years should usually be…
    - A) Mostly in equity
    - B) All in safe options
    - C) In crypto
    - D) In one stock
2. Target 60% equity; actual 68%. With a 5-point rule, what do you do first?
    - A) Do nothing ever
    - B) Send new money to debt (and gold) until it is back near target
    - C) Buy more equity
    - D) Sell everything
3. Which is an example of diversification?
    - A) All savings in one co-op society
    - B) An index fund holding many companies, plus deposits and some gold
    - C) All savings in one company's shares
    - D) Five funds holding the same stocks
4. Your EPF balance belongs to which asset class?
    - A) Debt
    - B) Equity
    - C) Real estate
    - D) Gold

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapter 15 on diversification and the NCFE long-term planning module
- **Action:** Set target allocations, build the Allocation tab with drift formulas and write your rebalancing rule. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Allocation tab with targets, actuals and the drift formula, and your rebalancing rule, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** There is no time to recover from a fall.
2. **B.** Drift is 8 points; new money first avoids selling.
3. **B.** Spreading across and within asset classes reduces the damage from any one failure.
4. **A.** It earns a declared interest rate; count it as debt in your allocation.

sections.title: Module 9: Investment options in India
sections.summary: Learn how each common investment in India works, what it costs, how it is taxed and what can go wrong, and compare options with official data, without anyone selling you anything.
sections.content:
## Overview

This is the longest module, because India offers many choices: mutual funds and index funds, post office schemes and deposits, EPF, PPF and NPS, shares, gold in several forms, REITs and property, and the Kerala favourites: KSFE chitties and co-operative deposits. Plus crypto, which you will be asked about.

The aim is not to pick products. It is to know, for each option, **what job it can do in your plan** (safety, income, growth, diversification), what it costs and how it can fail. You build a fund-comparison sheet from official data, check every adviser and tip source against SEBI's list, and write rules for gold, stocks, chitties and crypto. All of it feeds your Investment Policy Statement in Module 17.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain mutual funds, direct vs regular plans and the long-term cost of expense ratios
- Compare funds with official data and verify an adviser's SEBI registration
- Choose safe options for short and medium goals by post-tax return
- Explain EPF, PPF and NPS rules and tax as of November 2026
- Describe the honest risks of stocks, F&O, gold forms, REITs, property, chitties, co-operative deposits and crypto

## Time

About 16 hours in total: 14 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 16–19.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M09-L01: Mutual funds and SIPs: how they work (about 2 hours)
2. FIN-M09-L02: Index funds, comparing funds with official data, and when to pay an adviser (about 2 hours 30 minutes)
3. FIN-M09-L03: Safe options: small savings, deposits and debt funds (about 2 hours)
4. FIN-M09-L04: Retirement accounts: EPF, PPF and NPS (about 2 hours)
5. FIN-M09-L05: Stocks and demat basics: ownership, costs and honest risks (about 2 hours)
6. FIN-M09-L06: Gold, REITs and real estate (about 2 hours)
7. FIN-M09-L07: KSFE chitty, co-operative societies and crypto: benefits and risks (about 2 hours)

## Module project: My investment shortlist, by job, not by product

1. Make one page called **Shortlist** in your workbook with four sections: safety (emergency and short goals), income (if needed), long-term growth, and diversifiers (gold, REITs).
2. For each section, write the type of option that fits (for example, "post office TD and RD", "broad equity index fund, direct plan", "PPF", "gold ETF") and the evidence: your comparisons from this module.
3. List what you have decided **not** to use and why (for example, F&O, digital gold, unregistered chitties, endowment plans).
4. Write your rules for single stocks, gold, chitties, co-op deposits and crypto in one place.
5. Don't buy anything new yet unless it is a safe option for a short goal. You will write your Investment Policy Statement in Module 17 first.

**Proof to record:** Your Shortlist page with evidence, exclusions and rules, saved in 09 Investing.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mutual funds | Can't explain them | Understands basics | Compared direct and regular, and three funds from official data |
| Safe options | Not matched to goals | Some goals matched | Every short and medium goal matched by post-tax return |
| Retirement accounts | Unknown | Listed | Balances, nominees and rules checked; fit decided |
| Risky options | Not considered | Some rules | Written rules for stocks, F&O, gold, chitties, co-ops and crypto |
| Advice | Follows tips | Some checks | Every adviser and tip source checked on SEBI's list |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Compare direct and regular plans of one fund (FIN-M09-L01).
- Match each short goal to a safe option using the rates table (FIN-M09-L03).
- Check your EPF/PPF/NPS nominees and balances (FIN-M09-L04).
- Check one tip source on SEBI's list (FIN-M09-L05).

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Direct vs regular plan | Same fund and manager; direct has no commission, so lower cost and higher NAV. |
| Where to check an adviser | SEBI's list of registered investment advisers. |
| Small savings rates, Oct–Dec 2026 | PPF 7.1%, NSC 7.7%, SCSS 8.2%, SSA 8.2%, MIS 7.4%, KVP 7.5%, RD 6.7%. |
| Debt fund tax (bought from April 2023) | Gains taxed at your slab, however long you hold. |
| EPF rate for 2025-26 | 8.25%. |
| NPS exit for non-government subscribers | Up to 80% lump sum, at least 20% annuity; full withdrawal if corpus ≤ ₹8 lakh. |
| F&O reality | About 91% of individual traders lost money in 2024-25 (SEBI). |
| Crypto tax | 30% plus surcharge and cess; only cost deductible; no loss set-off; 1% TDS above limits. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Starting with products instead of jobs.** Decide what each rupee is for, then choose the type of option.
- **Trusting "safe" labels.** Check what actually protects the money: government backing, insurance, regulation, or nothing.
- **Doing everything at once.** Most people need only a few options: a safe place, a retirement account and a diversified growth option.

sections.title: FIN-M09-L01: Mutual funds and SIPs: how they work
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain how a mutual fund works, the difference between direct and regular plans, what the expense ratio costs you over 20 years, and how SIPs, KYC and statements work. **Time:** about 2 hours (30 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 60 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### What a mutual fund is

A **mutual fund** pools money from many investors and invests it in shares, bonds or other assets, managed by an **asset management company (AMC)** and regulated by SEBI. You buy **units**; the price of one unit is the **NAV** (net asset value), worked out every business day after expenses. If the fund's holdings rise, the NAV rises.

Main families of funds:

- **Equity funds:** mostly shares. Higher long-term potential, big ups and downs.
- **Debt funds:** bonds and money-market instruments. Lower ups and downs, with interest-rate and credit risk (FIN-M09-L03).
- **Hybrid funds:** a mix.
- **Index funds and ETFs:** copy a market index instead of picking stocks (FIN-M09-L02).
- **ELSS (tax-saver) funds:** equity funds with a **three-year lock-in**, counted per instalment for SIPs ([Edelweiss Mutual Fund](https://www.edelweissmf.com/investor-insights/mutual-fund-investment-tips-and-articles/elss-lock-in-period)); their tax deduction (section 123, the old 80C) is available only under the old tax regime.

### Direct and regular plans

Every scheme comes in two plans with **the same portfolio and the same fund manager** ([AMFI](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/Direct-Plan.html)):

- **Regular plan:** bought through a distributor (an agent, a bank, some apps), who is paid a commission from your money every year.
- **Direct plan:** bought straight from the fund house, without commission, so its **expense ratio is lower and its NAV higher**. You can invest directly through the fund house's website or office, the exchange platforms, MF Utility or the registrar's offices. Banks act as distributors, so bank portals don't sell direct plans.

AMFI says direct plans suit people who can choose funds themselves; if you want advice, a fee-only SEBI-registered investment adviser (FIN-M09-L02) is the alternative to commission-based selling.

### The expense ratio: the fee you never see

The **total expense ratio (TER)** is the yearly cost of running the fund, as a percentage of your money: management, registrar, custody, audit, marketing and other costs. It is taken out every day before the NAV is published, so you never see a bill. Funds must publish their TER daily on their websites and AMFI's website ([AMFI](https://amfiindia.com/investor-corner/knowledge-center/Expense-Ratio.html)). SEBI announced in December 2025 a new **base expense ratio** framework from 1 April, with caps for open-ended equity schemes falling from 2.10% for the smallest funds to 0.95% for the largest, and statutory levies such as STT shown separately ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/markets/news/sebi-revamps-mf-expense-ratio-framework-125121700968_1.html), check current rules).

**Worked example:** ₹5,000 a month for 20 years. If the fund's investments earn 10% a year before costs, a 0.3% expense ratio leaves 9.7% and a 1.3% expense ratio leaves 8.7%. The results: about **₹36,81,910** versus **₹32,38,269**. One percentage point of cost takes away about **₹4,43,642**, from ₹12,00,000 invested.

### SIPs

A **systematic investment plan** invests a fixed amount on a fixed date each month. It builds the habit, removes the temptation to "time the market", and buys more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high. It doesn't guarantee profit; in a falling market, a SIP also falls.

### KYC, statements and safety

- **KYC** is done once with PAN and Aadhaar-based verification or documents.
- **CAS:** a consolidated account statement lists every fund you hold, by PAN, each month you transact; you can request one from the registrars or MFCentral ([AMFI](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/cas.html)). It also shows nomination and KYC status.
- **Nominees:** for demat accounts and fund folios, up to three nominees under SEBI's circular of 29 May 2026, effective 1 September 2026 (Module 13).
- **Paying safely:** SEBI-registered intermediaries now collect money through **"@valid" UPI handles** (fund houses use ".mf"), and you can verify a UPI ID or bank account with **SEBI Check** before paying ([Moneylife](https://www.moneylife.in/article/sebi-launches-at-valid-upi-handles-and-checking-tool-to-curb-payment-frauds/78469.html)).
- Past returns don't guarantee future returns, and no mutual fund guarantees returns.

## Local example

**Fathima's** bank relationship manager suggested "a top-rated fund" for ₹3,000 a month. She looked it up on the fund house's website and found two NAVs for the same scheme: the regular plan and the direct plan. The factsheet showed a TER of 1.62% for regular and 0.58% for direct (made-up numbers for this example).

She asked the manager why he hadn't mentioned the direct plan. He said, honestly, that the bank sells regular plans and is paid by the fund house. Fathima thanked him and decided that she would choose funds herself using FIN-M09-L02, and invest only after writing her Investment Policy Statement (Module 17). "The same fund, the same manager, a 1% difference every year for 20 years," she wrote. "That's my money, not a detail."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AMFI: direct plans explained](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/Direct-Plan.html) | Direct and regular plans: what is the same, what differs, and how to invest directly | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AMFI: what the total expense ratio is, and where it is disclosed](https://amfiindia.com/investor-corner/knowledge-center/Expense-Ratio.html) | What the expense ratio covers and where it is disclosed | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Zerodha Varsity: all modules](https://zerodha.com/varsity/modules/) | Module 11, "Personal Finance: Mutual Funds": the first chapters on how funds work | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AMFI: consolidated account statement (CAS)](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/cas.html) | How the consolidated account statement works | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Moneylife: SEBI's @valid UPI handles and SEBI Check (October 2025)](https://www.moneylife.in/article/sebi-launches-at-valid-upi-handles-and-checking-tool-to-curb-payment-frauds/78469.html) | The @valid UPI handles and SEBI Check | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Pick any one well-known equity index fund (as a learning example, not a recommendation). On its fund house's website, find the direct and regular plans and write down both NAVs and both TERs.
2. Put the two TERs into the expense calculator template with your own SIP amount and 20 years, and write the difference in rupees.
3. If you already hold mutual funds, request your CAS and check which plan (direct or regular) each holding is, and its nomination status.
4. Write down how you would pay safely: through the fund house's official site or app, and checking the @valid UPI handle.
5. Write three sentences explaining a mutual fund, a SIP and the expense ratio to a family member.

**Proof to record:** Your direct-vs-regular comparison (NAVs, TERs and the rupee difference over 20 years) and, if you have funds, your CAS check, saved in 09 Investing.

## Template: expense ratio calculator

```
B2: monthly SIP (₹)                      5000
B3: years                                20
B4: return before costs (e.g. 0.10)      0.10
B5: expense ratio, plan A (e.g. 0.003)   0.003
B6: expense ratio, plan B (e.g. 0.013)   0.013
B7: value with plan A  =FV((B4-B5)/12,B3*12,-B2,0,1)
B8: value with plan B  =FV((B4-B6)/12,B3*12,-B2,0,1)
B9: cost of the difference  =B7-B8
```

## Common mistakes

- **Buying a regular plan without knowing it.** Check the plan name on your statement; "Direct" appears in direct plans.
- **Judging a fund by last year's return.** One good year says little. FIN-M09-L02 shows what to compare.
- **Ignoring the expense ratio.** It is taken every day, every year. Small percentages become lakhs over decades.
- **Paying to unknown UPI IDs or accounts.** Use official channels and check @valid handles or SEBI Check.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the difference between direct and regular plans of the same scheme?
    - A) Same portfolio and manager; direct has no distributor commission, so a lower expense ratio
    - B) Regular plans are guaranteed
    - C) Different portfolios
    - D) Direct plans are riskier
2. How is the expense ratio charged?
    - A) Deducted daily before the NAV is published
    - B) As a yearly bill
    - C) It is never charged
    - D) Only when you sell
3. What is the lock-in of an ELSS fund, for a SIP?
    - A) Five years
    - B) No lock-in
    - C) Three years for each instalment
    - D) Three years from the first instalment only
4. Where can you see all your mutual funds in one statement?
    - A) A consolidated account statement (CAS)
    - B) Your credit report
    - C) Form 16
    - D) Your bank passbook

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** AMFI on direct plans and expense ratios, Varsity's mutual fund basics, the CAS and safe payments
- **Action:** Compare a fund's direct and regular plans and calculate the 20-year cost of the difference. It is done when your proof is saved: your direct-vs-regular comparison (NAVs, TERs and the rupee difference over 20 years) and, if you have funds, your CAS check, saved in 09 Investing.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** Only the cost (and so the NAV) differs.
2. **A.** You don't see it; it reduces the NAV every day.
3. **C.** Each unit is locked for three years from its allotment.
4. **A.** The CAS lists all your holdings by PAN.

sections.title: FIN-M09-L02: Index funds, comparing funds with official data, and when to pay an adviser
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare mutual funds using official data (category, plan, expense ratio, riskometer, returns against the benchmark) in a fund-comparison sheet, and know when and how to use a SEBI-registered investment adviser. **Time:** about 2 hours 30 minutes (30 minutes reading, 40 minutes resources, 80 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Active and passive funds

- An **active fund** has a manager who picks stocks to try to beat a benchmark index. Higher costs; some years it beats the index, many years it doesn't.
- An **index fund** (or index ETF) simply holds the shares in an index, such as the Nifty 50 or the Sensex, in the same proportions. Low costs, no manager skill needed, and you get the market's return minus a small cost. The gap between the fund's return and its index is the **tracking difference**; lower is better.

Many beginners start long-term equity investing with a broad index fund because it is cheap, diversified and easy to understand. This course doesn't tell you which fund to buy; it shows you how to compare.

### What to compare, and where to find it

Use **official sources**: the fund's **factsheet**, the **scheme information document** and the **Key Information Memorandum** on the fund house's website, and AMFI's website for expense ratios.

| What | Why it matters | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Category | Compare like with like: a large-cap fund with large-cap funds | Factsheet, scheme documents |
| Plan | Direct plans cost less | Scheme name |
| Expense ratio (TER) | The cost you pay every year | Fund website, AMFI website |
| Riskometer | SEBI's six-level risk scale | Factsheet |
| Benchmark | The index the fund should be judged against | Factsheet |
| Returns vs benchmark over 3, 5 and 10 years | Consistency matters more than one great year | Factsheet |
| Tracking difference (index funds) | How closely it follows the index after costs | Factsheet or fund website |
| Fund size (AUM) and age | Very small or very new funds have less history | Factsheet |
| Exit load | A charge for selling early | Scheme documents |
| Portfolio | What it actually owns; overlap with your other funds | Factsheet, monthly portfolio |

**What not to use as the main guide:** star ratings, "top fund" lists, social media posts, and last year's return.

### When to pay for advice

You can manage simple investments yourself with this course. Consider a **SEBI-registered investment adviser (RIA)** when the sums are large, your situation is complex (business income, a big inheritance, NRI status, retirement), or you want a second opinion on your plan.

- **RIAs charge a fee** and must not earn commissions from products they recommend. SEBI caps their fees: a fixed fee of up to about ₹1.51 lakh per family per year, or up to 2.5% a year of the assets they advise on ([Cafemutual, January 2025](https://cafemutual.com/news/industry/33937-rias-can-now-charge-fees-up-to-rs-151-lakh-per-family-in-fixed-fees), check current rules).
- **Verify registration** on SEBI's website before paying anyone: search the [list of registered investment advisers](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/other/OtherAction.do?doRecognisedFpi=yes&intmId=13) by name or registration number, and match the details. SEBI has long asked people to deal only with registered advisers and research analysts and to beware of tips by SMS and social media ([SEBI](https://www.sebi.gov.in/media/press-releases/jun-2016/sebi-cautions-public-to-deal-with-only-sebi-registered-investment-advisers-and-research-analysts_32627.html)).
- **Finfluencers:** since 2024, SEBI-regulated entities can't have any association with unregistered people who give advice or make return claims ([Business Today, August 2024](https://www.businesstoday.in/amp/personal-finance/investment/story/sebi-tweaks-regulations-for-finfluencers-removes-content-of-over-15000-unregulated-entities-443789-2024-08-31)). A YouTuber or Telegram channel recommending specific funds or stocks for money must be registered; most aren't.
- A distributor (an agent paid by commission) can sell you products but is not an adviser; ask how they are paid.
- **Learn more, free:** SEBI's **Saa₹thi** app (launched in January 2022) is its mobile app for investor education ([SEBI press release](https://www.sebi.gov.in/media/press-releases/jan-2022/sebi-chairman-launches-saa-thi-sebi-s-mobile-app-on-investor-education_55384.html)); NSE runs free investor awareness programmes and publishes study material ([NSE](https://www.nseindia.com/invest/investors-awareness-programs)).

## Local example

**Anu** practised comparing three index funds that track the same index (names hidden here; she used real ones from fund house websites, as a learning exercise):

|  | Fund 1 (direct) | Fund 2 (direct) | Fund 3 (direct) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Category | Index fund | Index fund | Index fund |
| Benchmark | Same index | Same index | Same index |
| Expense ratio | 0.20% | 0.45% | 0.18% |
| Riskometer | Very High | Very High | Very High |
| Tracking difference, 1 year | −0.25% | −0.60% | −0.40% |
| Fund age | 8 years | 3 years | 1 year |
| Exit load | None | None | None |

(The numbers are made up for the example.) Fund 3 was cheapest, but too new to judge its tracking. Fund 2 cost more and tracked worse. Fund 1 had a long, close-tracking record. She noted that all three were "Very High" on the riskometer, like all equity funds, which is why only her long-term money (FIN-M08-L03) would go into equity. She didn't buy yet; the comparison goes into her Investment Policy Statement in Module 17.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [SEBI investor website: riskometer](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html) | How to read the riskometer in a factsheet | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AMFI: what the total expense ratio is, and where it is disclosed](https://amfiindia.com/investor-corner/knowledge-center/Expense-Ratio.html) | Where expense ratios are published | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Cafemutual: SEBI fee limits for registered investment advisers (January 2025)](https://cafemutual.com/news/industry/33937-rias-can-now-charge-fees-up-to-rs-151-lakh-per-family-in-fixed-fees) | SEBI's fee limits for registered investment advisers | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [SEBI: list of registered investment advisers (search by name or number)](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/other/OtherAction.do?doRecognisedFpi=yes&intmId=13) | Search the list of registered investment advisers; try searching one name you have seen online | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Business Today: SEBI rules on finfluencers (August 2024)](https://www.businesstoday.in/amp/personal-finance/investment/story/sebi-tweaks-regulations-for-finfluencers-removes-content-of-over-15000-unregulated-entities-443789-2024-08-31) | SEBI's rules on finfluencers | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Zerodha Varsity: all modules](https://zerodha.com/varsity/modules/) | Module 11, "Personal Finance: Mutual Funds": the chapters on index funds and choosing funds | 40 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Funds** tab with the template.
2. Choose a category that fits your long-term allocation (for example, a broad equity index fund) and find three funds in it.
3. Fill in every column from official documents only: factsheets, scheme documents and the fund websites. Note the date of each factsheet.
4. Use the formulas to compare returns with the benchmark.
5. Write which fund ranks best on your criteria and why, without buying.
6. Search SEBI's adviser list for any adviser, finfluencer or "guru" whose advice you have followed or considered. Write whether they are registered.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Funds tab with three funds compared from official data (with factsheet dates) and your SEBI registration check, saved in 09 Investing.

## Template: Funds tab

```
Row 1: Fund name,Plan (Direct/Regular),Category,Benchmark,Expense ratio %,Riskometer,AUM (₹ crore),Fund age (years),Exit load,3-yr return %,3-yr benchmark %,Difference,5-yr return %,5-yr benchmark %,Difference,Factsheet date,Notes
L2: =J2-K2      O2: =M2-N2
Cheapest: =INDEX(A2:A10,MATCH(MIN(E2:E10),E2:E10,0))
Average expense ratio: =AVERAGE(E2:E10)
```

## Template: adviser check

```
Name and firm: ____
SEBI registration number (from them): ____
Found on SEBI's list? Yes / No   Details match (name, address)? Yes / No
How are they paid? Fixed fee / % of assets / commission
Do they promise returns? (a red flag) Yes / No
```

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing by star ratings or last year's return.** Compare category, cost, risk and long-term returns against the benchmark.
- **Comparing funds from different categories.** A small-cap fund and a large-cap fund aren't competitors; compare within a category.
- **Following unregistered tipsters.** Check SEBI's list. No registration, no advice.
- **Owning many similar funds.** Several funds with the same holdings add complexity, not diversification.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the best way to judge an equity fund's returns?
    - A) Its star rating
    - B) Its advertisements
    - C) Against its benchmark over 3, 5 and 10 years
    - D) Last year's return only
2. How can you check that an investment adviser is genuine?
    - A) Search SEBI's list of registered investment advisers
    - B) Ask in a WhatsApp group
    - C) Check their follower count
    - D) Trust a certificate they send
3. What is the fee cap for SEBI-registered investment advisers, as of November 2026?
    - A) No limit
    - B) ₹500 per tip
    - C) About ₹1.51 lakh per family per year fixed, or 2.5% of assets advised
    - D) 10% of profits
4. Why do many beginners start with a broad index fund?
    - A) It has no risk
    - B) It is low-cost, diversified and simple to understand
    - C) It is guaranteed
    - D) It never falls

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The riskometer, expense ratio disclosure, RIA fees, SEBI's adviser list, finfluencer rules and Varsity's fund-choice chapters
- **Action:** Compare three funds in one category from official data in a Funds tab and check one adviser's registration. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Funds tab with three funds compared from official data (with factsheet dates) and your SEBI registration check, saved in 09 Investing.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Consistency against the right benchmark matters most.
2. **A.** SEBI's list is the official record of registration.
3. **C.** SEBI set these limits in January 2025 (check current rules).
4. **B.** It still carries market risk (Very High on the riskometer) but is cheap and diversified.

sections.title: FIN-M09-L03: Safe options: small savings, deposits and debt funds
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare post office small savings schemes, bank deposits and debt mutual funds on rate, safety, lock-in and tax, and choose the right one for each short or medium goal. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 65 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Small savings schemes

These schemes are run by the Government of India through post offices and authorised banks; interest rates are set every quarter. Rates for **October to December 2026** (unchanged for the tenth quarter in a row) ([Indian Bank table](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/), [Free Press Journal](https://www.freepressjournal.in/business/small-savings-interest-rates-unchanged-for-oct-dec-ppf-at-71-per-cent-nsc-at-77-pc), check current rules):

| Scheme | Rate | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Post office savings account | 4.0% | Basic account |
| Recurring deposit (5 years) | 6.7% | From ₹100 a month |
| Time deposit (1, 2, 3, 5 years) | 6.9%, 7.0%, 7.1%, 7.5% | The 5-year TD qualifies for the old-regime section 123 deduction |
| Monthly Income Scheme (MIS) | 7.4% | Monthly interest; up to ₹9 lakh single, ₹15 lakh joint |
| National Savings Certificate (NSC) | 7.7% | 5 years; interest paid at maturity |
| Kisan Vikas Patra (KVP) | 7.5% | Money doubles in 115 months |
| Public Provident Fund (PPF) | 7.1% | 15 years; tax-free interest (FIN-M09-L04) |
| Sukanya Samriddhi (SSA) | 8.2% | For a girl child; ₹250 to ₹1.5 lakh a year |
| Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS) | 8.2% | For 60+; up to ₹30 lakh; quarterly interest |

Limits are from [Outlook Money (January 2024)](https://www.outlookmoney.com/retirement/invest/fd-small-savings/post-office-small-savings-schemes-know-the-interest-rates-and-key-features) and [India Post](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving); check current limits before you invest. Interest on most of these is **taxable at your slab** (PPF and SSA are the main exceptions), and the government backing means very low credit risk.

### Bank FDs

Covered in FIN-M04-L03: rates vary by bank, ₹5 lakh deposit insurance per bank, taxed at your slab, penalties for breaking early.

### Debt mutual funds

Debt funds lend to governments and companies. Types include overnight and liquid funds (very short loans), short-duration funds, corporate bond funds and gilt funds (government bonds).

- **Interest-rate risk:** when interest rates rise, existing bonds lose value, so debt fund NAVs dip; longer-duration funds dip more.
- **Credit risk:** a borrower may fail to repay; funds that chase higher yields hold riskier borrowers.
- **Tax:** units of "specified mutual funds" (investing more than 65% in debt) bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed as **short-term gains at your slab rate, however long you hold them** (section 76 of the Income-tax Act, 2025) ([section 76](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-76-106), check current rules). So their old tax advantage over FDs is gone; compare them on liquidity and post-tax return.

For most beginners, **post office schemes and insured bank deposits** cover short and medium goals simply. Debt funds become useful when amounts grow and you understand their risks.

### Choosing by goal

| Goal | Good fits | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergency fund | Savings account + FD ladder (Module 5) | Access within a day |
| Sinking funds (yearly costs) | RD matching the date | Monthly deposits, known maturity |
| 1–5 year goals | Post office TD, NSC, FDs, RDs | Safety and a known return |
| Parents' regular income | SCSS (60+), MIS, payout FDs | Regular interest, government backing |
| Daughter's education | SSA, alongside other long-term options | High fixed rate, long term |

### Post-tax return

Compare what you keep: **post-tax return = rate × (1 − your tax slab)**. At 7.5% and a 20% slab, you keep 6%. For someone with no taxable income, the full 7.5%.

## Local example

**Joseph and Mary** (both over 60) wanted monthly income from ₹10 lakh of savings. With their son, they compared, using the October to December 2026 rates:

| Option | Rate | Yearly interest on the amount | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SCSS, ₹8 lakh in Joseph's name | 8.2% | ₹65,600 | Quarterly payout; within the ₹30 lakh limit |
| Post office MIS, ₹2 lakh in Mary's name | 7.4% | ₹14,800 | Monthly payout |
| Total |  | ₹80,400 a year, about ₹6,700 a month | Both government-backed |

Their earlier plan, one big FD at a co-operative society, would have paid a little more but without deposit insurance (FIN-M04-L03). They kept ₹1 lakh in an FD ladder at their bank as an emergency fund, and noted that the SCSS rate is fixed for an account when opened, while rates for new accounts change every quarter.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [India Post: saving schemes and current interest rates](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving) | The current interest rates for every post office scheme | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Indian Bank: small savings interest rates, October to December 2026](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/) | The quarterly rates table for October to December 2026 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Outlook Money: post office schemes, deposit limits and features (January 2024)](https://www.outlookmoney.com/retirement/invest/fd-small-savings/post-office-small-savings-schemes-know-the-interest-rates-and-key-features) | Deposit limits and features of each scheme (January 2024) | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Income-tax Act, 2025, section 76: gains on debt-oriented mutual funds](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-76-106) | Section 76: why debt fund gains are now taxed at your slab | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [AMFI: tax corner (how mutual funds are taxed)](https://amfiindia.com/investor-corner/knowledge-center/tax-corner.html) | AMFI's tax corner: how debt and other funds are taxed | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. List your short and medium goals from the Goals tab (horizon under 7 years).
2. For each, choose two possible options from this lesson and compare them in the template: rate, lock-in, safety, tax and post-tax return.
3. Check the current quarter's rates on India Post's page, as rates may have changed since November 2026.
4. Pick the option for each goal and add it to the "Where the money waits" column in your Goals tab.
5. If you help parents or grandparents with money, check whether SCSS or MIS could fit their needs and write it down for a family conversation.

**Proof to record:** Your safe-options comparison with post-tax returns and the updated "Where the money waits" column, saved in 09 Investing.

## Template: safe options comparison

```
Row 1: Goal,Option,Rate (e.g. 0.075),Lock-in or tenure,Safety (govt / insured bank / fund),Taxed at slab? (Yes/No),My slab (e.g. 0.05),Post-tax rate %,Decision
H2: =IF(F2="Yes",C2*(1-G2),C2)*100
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring tax on interest.** Compare post-tax returns, especially if your slab is 20% or 30%.
- **Thinking debt funds are "like FDs".** Their NAV can fall when rates rise or a borrower defaults.
- **Locking money in a long scheme for a short goal.** Match the lock-in to the goal date.
- **Using old rates.** Small savings rates change quarterly for new deposits. Check before investing.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What was the PPF interest rate for October to December 2026?
    - A) 7.1%
    - B) 8.2%
    - C) 12%
    - D) 4%
2. How are gains on a debt mutual fund bought after 1 April 2023 taxed?
    - A) At a flat 1%
    - B) At 12.5% after 2 years
    - C) As short-term gains at your slab rate, however long you hold
    - D) Always tax-free
3. A deposit pays 7.5% and your slab is 20%. What is the post-tax return?
    - A) 7.5%
    - B) 6%
    - C) 5.5%
    - D) 9%
4. Which scheme is meant for people aged 60 and above?
    - A) KVP
    - B) NSC
    - C) Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS)
    - D) Sukanya Samriddhi

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Current small savings rates and limits, section 76 and AMFI's tax corner
- **Action:** Choose a safe option for each short and medium goal by comparing post-tax returns. It is done when your proof is saved: your safe-options comparison with post-tax returns and the updated "Where the money waits" column, saved in 09 Investing.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** PPF stayed at 7.1% (check current rates).
2. **C.** Section 76 treats specified mutual fund gains as short-term.
3. **B.** 7.5 × (1 − 0.2) = 6%.
4. **C.** SCSS paid 8.2% in October to December 2026, with quarterly interest.

sections.title: FIN-M09-L04: Retirement accounts: EPF, PPF and NPS
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain how EPF, PPF and NPS work, their withdrawal rules and tax treatment as of November 2026, and decide which fit your work situation. **Time:** about 2 hours (30 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 60 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

These three accounts are designed for the long term, with rules that make early withdrawal hard. That is a feature: they protect retirement money from today's wants.

### EPF (Employees' Provident Fund)

For employees of establishments covered by EPFO: you and your employer contribute every month from your salary.

- **Interest:** 8.25% for 2025-26, the third year in a row at that rate ([Business Today, July 2026](https://www.businesstoday.in/personal-finance/story/your-epf-balance-is-about-to-rise-epfo-orders-8-25-interest-credit-541245-2026-07-06)).
- **Withdrawals (from October 2025):** 13 rules were merged into 3 categories: essential needs (illness, education, marriage), housing, and special circumstances. Members can withdraw **up to 100% of the eligible balance**, but **25% of contributions must stay** in the account; the minimum service is 12 months; education withdrawals are allowed up to 10 times and marriage up to 5. After leaving a job, **full withdrawal (premature final settlement) needs 12 months** without a job (earlier 2 months), and the pension part (EPS) **36 months** ([Onmanorama, October 2025](https://www.onmanorama.com/news/business/2025/10/14/epfo-partial-withdrawal-rules-change.html), check current rules).
- **Voluntary PF (VPF):** you can contribute extra to EPF through your employer.
- **Change jobs, keep the account:** transfer your balance to the new employer instead of withdrawing; withdrawing early is the most common way people lose retirement savings.

### PPF (Public Provident Fund)

Open to anyone, at a post office or bank ([Central Bank of India](https://centralbank.bank.in/en/node/223409), check current rules):

- **₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh a year**, one account per person; 7.1% for October to December 2026.
- **15 years**, extendable in 5-year blocks.
- **Partial withdrawal** once a year after 5 years (up to 50% of an earlier balance); **premature closure** after 5 years only for serious illness, higher education or a change to NRI status, with 1% less interest.
- **Interest is tax-free**, and deposits count for the section 123 deduction under the old regime.
- If you miss the ₹500 minimum in a year, the account is "discontinued" and can be revived with a small penalty.

### NPS (National Pension System)

Regulated by PFRDA, open to citizens aged 18 to 85 ([SBI's NPS page](https://sbi.bank.in/web/personal-banking/investments-deposits/govt-schemes/nps), check current rules):

- **Tier I** (the pension account with tax benefits and withdrawal limits) and **Tier II** (optional, flexible, no tax benefit). ₹250 to open.
- You choose a pension fund manager and how much goes to equity, corporate bonds and government bonds (or an automatic mix by age), and can change them during the year.
- **Tax:** an extra ₹50,000 deduction under the old regime (the old "80CCD(1B)"), on top of the ₹1.5 lakh limit; **employer contributions** are deductible up to 10% of basic plus DA in the old regime and 14% in the new regime.
- **Exit rules for non-government subscribers (December 2025 changes):** at normal exit, up to **80% as a lump sum** and at least **20% in an annuity** (it was 60:40); if the corpus is ₹8 lakh or less, you can take it all ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/personal-finance/pfrda-allows-financial-assistance-against-nps-corpus-under-exit-rule-tweaks-125121601190_1.html), check current rules). Partial withdrawals are allowed for specific needs such as a house or medical treatment.
- **Tax on the lump sum:** only **60% is explicitly tax-free**; the record-keeper notes that the extra 20% is taxable at your slab unless the government clarifies otherwise ([Protean](https://proteantech.in/articles/nps-withdrawal-rules-2025-changes-december/), check current rules).

Government employees have their own NPS rules (Module 14).

### Which fits you?

| Situation | Typical fit |
| --- | --- |
| Salaried in a covered private job | EPF (automatic), perhaps VPF; NPS through the employer if offered |
| Freelancer, business owner, PSC aspirant | PPF as a safe base; NPS for long-term growth with a lock-in |
| Kerala government employee | NPS (contributory pension) and GPF rules from Module 14 |
| Low income, no tax | PPF for safety and flexibility; the Atal Pension Yojana (Module 12) |

## Local example

**Fathima** has no employer, so no EPF. She had a PPF account opened by her father when she was 20, with irregular deposits; one year had no deposit, so the account was discontinued. She revived it at the post office with the small penalty and the missed ₹500.

She decided on two retirement accounts: **PPF**, with ₹2,000 a month by standing instruction, as the safe base (tax-free interest, government-backed); and **NPS Tier I** for growth, with ₹1,500 a month, once she finishes Module 12. She read the exit rules carefully: most of the NPS money is locked until 60, which she sees as protection from herself in good freelance years.

Her note: "EPF rules changed in 2025 and NPS rules in December 2025. I'll check both every year in my review."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Central Bank of India: PPF rules](https://centralbank.bank.in/en/node/223409) | PPF rules: limits, maturity, withdrawals, closure and revival | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Onmanorama: EPFO allows up to 100% partial withdrawal (October 2025)](https://www.onmanorama.com/news/business/2025/10/14/epfo-partial-withdrawal-rules-change.html) | The October 2025 EPF withdrawal changes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Business Today: EPF interest of 8.25% for 2025-26 (July 2026)](https://www.businesstoday.in/personal-finance/story/your-epf-balance-is-about-to-rise-epfo-orders-8-25-interest-credit-541245-2026-07-06) | EPF interest for 2025-26 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SBI: National Pension System (NPS)](https://sbi.bank.in/web/personal-banking/investments-deposits/govt-schemes/nps) | NPS: tiers, contributions, tax benefits and exit summary | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Business Standard: new NPS exit and withdrawal rules (December 2025)](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/personal-finance/pfrda-allows-financial-assistance-against-nps-corpus-under-exit-rule-tweaks-125121601190_1.html) | The December 2025 NPS exit and withdrawal changes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Zerodha Varsity: all modules](https://zerodha.com/varsity/modules/) | Module 17, "NPS: National Pension System": the first chapters | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Write down which of EPF, PPF and NPS you already have. For EPF, check your passbook through EPFO's online member services (or ask your employer); for PPF, your passbook; for NPS, your statement.
2. For each account you have, check: nominee, last contribution, balance. Add them to your Net Worth and Allocation tabs (as debt, or split for NPS).
3. For the accounts you don't have, write whether they fit you, using the table.
4. Write one rule about your EPF if you have one, for example: "When I change jobs, I transfer my EPF; I never withdraw it for wants."
5. Note the next check date for these rules in your yearly review.

**Proof to record:** Your retirement accounts summary (accounts held, balances, nominees, fit for the others) and your EPF rule, saved in 09 Investing.

## Template: retirement accounts summary

```csv
Account,Have it? (Yes/No),Balance (₹),Monthly contribution (₹),Nominee updated?,Withdrawal rule I must remember,Fits me? Why
EPF,,,,,"12 months' service; 25% stays; final settlement after 12 months without a job",
VPF,,,,,,
PPF,,,,,"15 years; ₹500 minimum each year; partial after 5 years",
NPS Tier I,,,,,"Mostly locked to 60; up to 80% lump sum, 20%+ annuity (non-govt)",
NPS Tier II,,,,,"Flexible; no tax benefit",
```

## Common mistakes

- **Withdrawing EPF when changing jobs.** Transfer it. Early withdrawal destroys decades of compounding.
- **Missing the ₹500 PPF minimum.** Set a standing instruction for at least ₹500 in April every year.
- **Choosing NPS only for the tax deduction.** Choose it if the lock-in and rules fit your retirement plan; the deduction is old-regime only.
- **Forgetting nominees on retirement accounts.** Check them now; Module 13 explains why.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What EPF interest rate was set for 2025-26?
    - A) 7.1%
    - B) 12%
    - C) 4%
    - D) 8.25%
2. Under the October 2025 EPF rules, how long after leaving a job before full withdrawal?
    - A) 12 months
    - B) 2 months
    - C) Never
    - D) 5 years
3. What is the PPF deposit range per year?
    - A) ₹100 to ₹50,000
    - B) ₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh
    - C) ₹10,000 minimum
    - D) No limit
4. After the December 2025 changes, how much can a non-government NPS subscriber take as a lump sum at normal exit?
    - A) 100% always
    - B) Up to 80%
    - C) Up to 40%
    - D) Nothing

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** PPF rules, EPF withdrawal changes and interest, NPS features and exit changes, and Varsity's NPS chapters
- **Action:** Summarise your EPF, PPF and NPS position, update nominees and balances, and write your EPF rule. It is done when your proof is saved: your retirement accounts summary (accounts held, balances, nominees, fit for the others) and your EPF rule, saved in 09 Investing.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **D.** It was 8.25%, the third year in a row.
2. **A.** Premature final settlement moved from 2 to 12 months.
3. **B.** One account per person, ₹500 minimum, ₹1.5 lakh maximum.
4. **B.** At least 20% goes to an annuity; full withdrawal only if the corpus is ₹8 lakh or less.
