sections.title: FIN-M10-L05: Freelancers and small businesses: presumptive tax and GST basics
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Decide whether presumptive taxation fits your freelance or business income, calculate your taxable income under it, and know when GST registration becomes necessary. **Time:** about 2 hours (30 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 60 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Business, profession or salary?

Tuition, freelance design, video editing, consulting, a home bakery: these are income from **business or profession**, not salary. You can either keep accounts and pay tax on actual profit (income minus expenses), or, if eligible, use **presumptive taxation**, which deems a fixed share of receipts to be your income, with much simpler records.

### Presumptive taxation (section 58 of the new Act)

([section 58](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-58-144), check current rules)

- **Small businesses** (resident individuals, HUFs and firms other than LLPs) with turnover up to **₹2 crore** (₹3 crore if cash receipts are no more than 5%): deemed profit is **6% of receipts through banking or digital modes plus 8% of other receipts**, or your actual profit if higher.
- **Specified professions** (listed in section 62(4)) with gross receipts up to **₹50 lakh** (₹75 lakh if cash receipts are no more than 5%): deemed income is **50% of receipts**, or actual if higher. Check whether your kind of work is on the list; if not, the business rule may apply.
- You don't need detailed books for the deemed income, but keep invoices and bank records. You can pay all advance tax by **15 March** (FIN-M10-L03).

**Worked example:** Fathima's receipts are ₹7,20,000 a year, all by bank transfer.

- If her work counts as a specified profession: deemed income 50% = ₹3,60,000.
- If it counts as a business: deemed profit 6% = ₹43,200.

Either way, her income plus about ₹20,000 of interest is far below ₹12 lakh, so under the new regime her tax is **₹0**. She still files, to claim back TDS her clients deducted and to keep a clean income record. (A tax practitioner helped her decide which rule applies to her work, which is worth paying for once.)

### GST: when do you need it?

GST is charged on most sales of goods and services. You must **register** when your **aggregate turnover** in a year crosses the limit: **₹20 lakh for services** (₹10 lakh in special category states), as per CBIC's registration guidance ([CBIC](https://cbic-gst.gov.in/pdf/press-release/registrtn-gst-regime.pdf), check current rules). Registration is online on the GST portal with PAN, email and mobile.

- After the GST Council's decisions effective **22 September 2025**, the main rates are **5%, 18% and 40%** ([GST Council](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-09/press_release_press_information_bureau.pdf), check current rules); many professional services are at 18%.
- Once registered, you charge GST on invoices, file regular GST returns and pay the GST collected (after input credits). **GST collected is not your income**: keep it aside in your holding account.
- Selling services to clients **outside India** (like Fathima's Gulf clients) follows special export rules; ask a GST practitioner before your turnover approaches the limit.
- Some situations need registration regardless of turnover. Check the rules for your exact business.

For business bookkeeping, GST invoices and income tax for a small business, the **Practical Entrepreneurship** course covers more (ENT-M08-L01 and ENT-M08-L03).

### Records that protect you

Keep for every payment: invoice number, client, date, amount, TDS deducted, how it was paid. Your holding account statement and invoice register are your proof if the department ever asks.

## Local example

**Nisha's Oven**, the home bakery in Kuttiady, sells cakes and snacks worth about ₹9 lakh a year, about 70% through UPI and 30% in cash. Nisha (the owner) compared presumptive and actual-profit taxation:

- **Presumptive (business):** 6% of ₹6,30,000 (digital) + 8% of ₹2,70,000 (cash) = ₹37,800 + ₹21,600 = **₹59,400** deemed profit.
- **Actual profit** from her records: about ₹1,80,000 after ingredients, gas, packaging and a helper's wages.

The presumptive figure is lower than her actual profit, and the rule says "6%/8% **or actual, if higher**", so her income for tax purposes is the higher figure, her actual ₹1,80,000. It is still well below the tax limit, so her tax is ₹0. The value of presumptive taxation for her is simpler records, not lower tax. And with ₹9 lakh of turnover in goods, she is below the GST limits for now; she put a reminder in her review to check when turnover approaches ₹20 lakh, and to confirm the limit for goods in Kerala.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Income-tax Act, 2025, section 58: presumptive taxation for small businesses and professionals](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-58-144) | Section 58: presumptive taxation limits and rates | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [CBIC: registration under GST (PDF)](https://cbic-gst.gov.in/pdf/press-release/registrtn-gst-regime.pdf) | When GST registration is required and how to register | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [GST Council: decisions of the 56th meeting (PDF, September 2025)](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-09/press_release_press_information_bureau.pdf) | The September 2025 GST rate changes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [ETV Bharat: over 7 crore returns filed for AY 2026-27 (31 August 2026)](https://www.etvbharat.com/en/business/over-7-crore-itrs-filed-for-ay27-deadline-ends-tonight-enn26083106916) | The 31 August due date for business and professional returns (news) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. If you have (or expect) freelance, tuition or business income, list last year's receipts by month and mode (digital or cash).
2. Calculate deemed income under the specified-profession rule and the business rule, and compare with your actual profit.
3. Write which rule you think applies to your work and what to confirm with a tax practitioner.
4. Add your yearly turnover to a GST watch line: the limit, your current turnover and the month you would cross it at your growth rate.
5. Set up an invoice register (template) if you don't have one.
6. No freelance income? Do steps 2 and 4 with Fathima's or Nisha's numbers, and note when you would need this.

**Proof to record:** Your presumptive-tax comparison, your GST watch line and your invoice register (or the worked practice), saved in 10 Tax.

## Template: presumptive tax comparison

```
B2: receipts by bank/digital (₹)     B3: receipts in cash (₹)     B4: actual profit from records (₹)
Business rule:      B6: =MAX(B2*0.06+B3*0.08,B4)
Profession rule:    B7: =MAX((B2+B3)*0.5,B4)     (only if your profession is listed in section 62(4))
Limits: business turnover up to ₹2 crore (₹3 crore if cash ≤ 5%); professional receipts up to ₹50 lakh (₹75 lakh if cash ≤ 5%)
Cash share:         B9: =IF(B2+B3>0,B3/(B2+B3)*100,0)
```

## Template: invoice register and GST watch

```
Invoice no,Date,Client,Description,Amount (₹),GST charged (₹),TDS deducted (₹),Received on,Mode (bank/UPI/cash)
GST watch: limit ₹2000000 (services; check yours) | turnover this year =SUM(E2:E200) | % of limit =SUM(E2:E200)/2000000*100
```

## Common mistakes

- **Assuming all freelance work is a "specified profession".** Check the list in section 62(4). If yours isn't on it, the business rule applies.
- **Thinking presumptive tax always lowers tax.** It is the deemed amount or actual profit, whichever is higher. Its main benefit is simpler records.
- **Spending GST you collected.** It belongs to the government. Keep it separate until you pay it.
- **Crossing the GST limit without noticing.** Track turnover monthly with the watch line.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Under the business presumptive rule, what is the deemed profit on ₹10 lakh received fully by UPI?
    - A) ₹0
    - B) ₹80,000 (8%)
    - C) ₹5 lakh (50%)
    - D) ₹60,000 (6%)
2. What is the deemed income for a specified profession with ₹8 lakh receipts?
    - A) ₹8 lakh
    - B) ₹48,000
    - C) ₹64,000
    - D) ₹4 lakh (50%)
3. When must a service provider in Kerala register for GST, per CBIC's guidance?
    - A) Only above ₹1 crore
    - B) From the first rupee
    - C) Never for freelancers
    - D) When aggregate turnover exceeds ₹20 lakh in a year
4. What should you do with GST collected from clients?
    - A) Invest it in shares
    - B) Return it to clients
    - C) Keep it aside and pay it to the government
    - D) Spend it as income

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Section 58, CBIC's GST registration guidance, the September 2025 GST changes and the business due date
- **Action:** Compare presumptive and actual tax on your freelance or business income and set up a GST watch and invoice register. It is done when your proof is saved: your presumptive-tax comparison, your GST watch line and your invoice register (or the worked practice), saved in 10 Tax.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **D.** 6% of digital receipts, unless actual profit is higher.
2. **D.** 50% of gross receipts, or actual if higher.
3. **D.** ₹20 lakh for services (₹10 lakh in special category states); check current rules and special cases.
4. **C.** GST collected is the government's money, held by you until you pay it.

sections.title: Module 11: Big life goals
sections.summary: Plan the big things life brings: a wedding, a vehicle, a home, children's education and support for your parents, with real numbers, without debt traps, and in agreement with your family.
sections.content:
## Overview

Big goals are where families most often borrow, pledge gold or sell land, usually because the cost arrived before the plan did. This module turns each one into a funded goal: a realistic cost, a future value, a monthly saving and a place for the money to wait, chosen by time horizon.

It also covers the decisions that numbers alone can't settle, such as whether to buy a house now or keep renting, how to talk about a wedding budget, and how siblings can share support for parents fairly. Your **Big Goals** tab becomes part of your final plan.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Turn weddings, vehicles and other big purchases into funded goals with total costs
- Compare renting and buying a home with several scenarios
- Plan a child's education with a saving mix, a glide path and backup options
- Map your parents' finances with them and close the dangerous gaps
- Agree family money decisions in writing

## Time

About 7 hours 30 minutes in total: 6 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 23–24.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M11-L01: Planning big goals: weddings, vehicles and sinking funds (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. FIN-M11-L02: A house: rent or buy? (about 2 hours)
3. FIN-M11-L03: Children's education (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
4. FIN-M11-L04: Supporting your parents (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Module project: My big goals plan

1. Complete the Big Goals tab: every big goal with future cost, monthly saving and where the money waits.
2. Add up the monthly savings for all big goals and compare with what your budget allows. Use the four levers (later, less, more income, drop) until it fits.
3. Attach your rent-or-buy decision and your parents' plan (or "not applicable now").
4. Update your Budget tab with the new monthly savings lines and your standing instructions.
5. Share the plan with the family members it affects.

**Proof to record:** Your Big Goals tab with totals that fit your budget, the rent-or-buy decision and the parents' plan, saved in 11 Big goals.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Costs | Guesses | Some quotes | Real costs, total cost of ownership where relevant, inflation applied |
| Funding | None | Monthly amounts, not in the budget | Monthly savings in the budget with standing instructions |
| House decision | Emotional only | One scenario | Three scenarios plus the four questions |
| Education | Not planned | Amount only | Saving mix, glide path and backup (or not applicable) |
| Family | Not discussed | Discussed | Agreed in writing with the people affected |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- List your big goals with costs and monthly savings (FIN-M11-L01).
- Answer the four house questions (FIN-M11-L02).
- Fill in the parents' money map, even partly (FIN-M11-L04).

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Total cost of ownership (vehicle) | EMI + insurance + fuel + servicing + running costs + loss of value. |
| Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 | Giving or taking dowry: at least 5 years' imprisonment and a fine. |
| Rent-or-buy comparison | Wealth after 10 years: house value minus loan left, vs investments from renting and investing the difference. |
| Four house questions | Will I stay 7–10 years? EMI under a third of pay? Legally clean, K-RERA registered? Fits my other goals? |
| Education inflation in this course's examples | 7% a year (an assumption). |
| Education glide path | Move education money step by step to safe options in the last 3–5 years. |
| First gap to close for parents | Health cover. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Planning big goals alone when the family pays.** Agree budgets with the people involved, in writing.
- **Borrowing for events and status.** Loans for celebrations and showy purchases delay every other goal.
- **Giving up retirement for children or parents.** Help others from a planned budget line, not from your future.

tasks.text: Module project: My big goals plan
tasks.detail: **Proof to record:** Your Big Goals tab with totals that fit your budget, the rent-or-buy decision and the parents' plan, saved in 11 Big goals.

tasks.text: Self-assessment: rubric scored, no row at 1

sections.title: FIN-M11-L01: Planning big goals: weddings, vehicles and sinking funds
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn a wedding, a vehicle or any big purchase into a funded goal with a real budget, a total cost of ownership and a monthly saving that fits your plan. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Big goals break budgets when they are treated as emergencies or as one-off "special" spending. Weddings, vehicles, house repairs and big family events are **known in advance**, so they can be planned like any other goal (Module 2): a price, a date, a monthly saving and a place for the money to wait (Modules 8 and 9).

### Weddings

Kerala weddings can cost several years of income: gold, the venue, food for hundreds of guests, clothes, photos and travel. Families often borrow, pledge gold or sell land for them.

- **Decide the budget before the planning starts,** together with the people paying, and write it down. Social pressure (Module 1) grows once relatives start suggesting.
- **List costs by category** and decide where to cut: a smaller venue, a shorter guest list, less gold.
- **Gold:** jewellery bought for a wedding is part of the family's wealth only at its buyback value (Module 2). Buying less, or holding part of it as gold ETFs, keeps more of the value.
- **Dowry is illegal.** Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking or helping with dowry is punishable with imprisonment of at least five years and a fine of at least ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more; presents given without any demand, listed and not excessive are excluded ([Ministry of Women and Child Development](https://wcd.nic.in/dowry-prohibition-act-1961-28-1961)). A financial plan should never include a dowry, and you have the law on your side if anyone demands one.
- **Don't borrow for the celebration.** Loans for a single day can take years to repay and delay every other goal.

### Vehicles: the total cost of ownership

The price is only the start. **Total cost of ownership** includes:

> **Monthly cost = EMI (or saving) + insurance ÷ 12 + fuel + servicing and repairs ÷ 12 + parking and tolls + the fall in value**

**Worked example:** a car priced ₹6,50,000 on road, 20% down, the rest as a 5-year loan at 9.5%: EMI ₹10,921. Add insurance (say ₹18,000 a year), fuel (₹4,000 a month) and servicing (₹12,000 a year), and it costs about **₹17,421 a month**, before the value it loses each year. A simple rule some people use: keep total vehicle costs under about 10–15% of take-home pay. Compare a two-wheeler, a used car or public transport honestly.

### Sinking funds for big goals

For each big goal: future cost (Module 2), monthly saving with PMT, and the right place for the money by time horizon:

- Under 3 years: RD, FDs, post office deposits.
- 3–7 years: mostly safe, with a small growth part, per your Investment Policy Statement.

When the goal arrives, the money is there, and nobody has to pledge gold.

## Local example

**Anu's** parents had always expected her wedding to cost "around ₹15 lakh, like her cousin's". Anu asked for a family meeting with the numbers from her Goals tab.

Together they listed what they really wanted: a simple ceremony at the local hall for 300 guests, a lunch, photos, and her grandmother's jewellery plus 5 new pavan. Their estimate came to about ₹7.5 lakh. Her parents had ₹4 lakh saved and the gold; Anu's share would be ₹1.5 lakh over four years, about ₹2,800 a month in an RD.

Two decisions changed the most: no new gold beyond the 5 pavan (her grandmother's jewellery mattered more to her), and no loan. When a relative asked about "what the groom's family expects", her father said firmly that the family doesn't do dowry. "Having the plan on paper made it easier to say no," he said afterwards.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Ministry of Women and Child Development: the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961](https://wcd.nic.in/dowry-prohibition-act-1961-28-1961) | The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961: what is prohibited, penalties and the exclusion for unrequested presents | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The long-term planning module (revision), with your big goals in mind | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Big Goals** tab with the template. List every big goal in the next 10 years: wedding, vehicle, house repairs, a family event, a business start-up, further study.
2. For each, write a realistic cost today, ideally from quotes or recent family experience.
3. For a vehicle goal, fill in the total cost of ownership calculator.
4. Use the formulas to get future cost and monthly saving; choose where each goal's money waits.
5. For any goal involving family (such as a wedding), share the numbers and agree a budget with the people paying. Write the agreed budget.

**Proof to record:** Your Big Goals tab with costs, monthly savings and places, a vehicle cost calculation if relevant, and the agreed budget for any family goal, saved in 11 Big goals.

## Template: Big Goals tab

```
Row 1: Goal,Cost today (₹),Years away,Inflation,Future cost (₹),Saved so far (₹),Return while saving,Monthly saving (₹),Where it waits,Who pays (me / family / shared),Agreed?
E2: =B2*(1+D2)^C2
H2: =IF(G2=0,(E2-F2)/(C2*12),PMT(G2/12,C2*12,-F2,E2)*-1)
```

## Template: vehicle total cost of ownership

```
B2: on-road price (₹)           B3: down payment (₹)       B4: loan rate (e.g. 0.095)    B5: loan months
B6: EMI (₹)                     =IF(B2-B3>0,PMT(B4/12,B5,-(B2-B3)),0)
B7: insurance per year (₹)      B8: fuel per month (₹)     B9: servicing per year (₹)    B10: parking, tolls per month (₹)
B11: monthly cost               =B6+B7/12+B8+B9/12+B10
B12: as % of take-home pay      =B11/take_home*100
```

## Common mistakes

- **Letting the guest list set the budget.** Set the budget first, then plan the event to fit it.
- **Comparing vehicles by EMI alone.** Insurance, fuel, servicing and depreciation often add more than half again.
- **Borrowing for a celebration.** A loan for one day can delay your goals for years.
- **Treating wedding gold as savings at the buying price.** Value it at the buyback rate; making charges are gone.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does "total cost of ownership" of a vehicle include?
    - A) Only the EMI
    - B) EMI, insurance, fuel, servicing, other running costs and loss of value
    - C) Only the on-road price
    - D) Only fuel
2. Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, what is the minimum prison term for giving or taking dowry?
    - A) Ten years
    - B) One month
    - C) There is none
    - D) Five years
3. A goal costs ₹3 lakh today, 4 years away, 5% inflation. About how much will it cost?
    - A) ₹4.5 lakh
    - B) ₹3 lakh
    - C) ₹3.65 lakh
    - D) ₹3.6 lakh exactly
4. When should the wedding budget be decided?
    - A) Before planning starts, with the people paying
    - B) After the wedding
    - C) Never; it is unpredictable
    - D) After the guest list is final

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Dowry Prohibition Act page and the NCFE long-term planning module
- **Action:** Build your Big Goals tab, calculate a vehicle's total cost if relevant, and agree a written budget for one family goal. It is done when your proof is saved: your Big Goals tab with costs, monthly savings and places, a vehicle cost calculation if relevant, and the agreed budget for any family goal, saved in 11 Big goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** All the costs of having the vehicle, not just buying it.
2. **D.** At least five years, plus a fine (the court can reduce it for special reasons).
3. **C.** ₹3,00,000 × 1.05⁴ ≈ ₹3,64,652.
4. **A.** A written budget first makes it easier to resist pressure later.

Action: Build your Big Goals tab, calculate a vehicle's total cost if relevant, and agree a written budget for one family goal

sections.title: FIN-M11-L02: A house: rent or buy?
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare renting and buying a home with a spreadsheet that includes the down payment, all costs, the EMI, the money you could invest instead, and your own assumptions. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Owning a home is deeply valued in Kerala, and it brings real security. It is also usually the biggest financial decision of a life. This lesson separates the **emotional** decision (where and how you want to live) from the **financial** one (what it costs compared with renting).

### The real costs of buying

- **Down payment:** banks lend only part of the value; you pay the rest from savings.
- **Stamp duty and registration:** set by the state, paid when you buy. Check the current rates with the Kerala registration department before planning.
- **Interiors, furniture, moving.**
- **The loan:** EMI for 15–25 years. On a floating rate, the EMI or tenure rises when rates rise (FIN-M06-L03); prepayment penalties aren't allowed on individuals' floating-rate home loans sanctioned from 2026 ([Angel One](https://www.angelone.in/news/personal-finance/rbi-new-rule-no-prepayment-penalty-on-floating-loans-from-jan-1-2026), check current rules).
- **Every year:** property tax, maintenance, repairs, home insurance (FIN-M07-L04).

### The costs of renting

Rent, rising over time, and a deposit. In exchange: flexibility (useful if your job may transfer you, as many government jobs do), no repairs, and the down payment and extra monthly money stay free to invest.

### A fair comparison

Compare **wealth after 10 years** under both choices:

- **Buy:** the house's value then, minus the loan still outstanding.
- **Rent:** invest the down payment and purchase costs, and every month invest the difference between the cost of owning (EMI plus upkeep) and the rent.

**Worked example** (made-up): a ₹40 lakh house, 20% down, 8% for stamp duty, registration and other costs, a ₹32 lakh loan at 8.5% for 20 years (EMI ₹27,770), upkeep ₹20,000 a year; rent of ₹12,000 a month rising 5% a year.

| Assumptions | Wealth after 10 years: buy | Wealth after 10 years: rent and invest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| House grows 4% a year; investments earn 8% | ₹36,81,175 | ₹51,96,891 |
| House grows 7% a year; investments earn 6% | ₹56,28,803 | ₹44,47,057 |

The answer **flips with the assumptions**. Nobody knows future house prices or investment returns, so test several. The rent path only wins if you **really invest the difference every month**; most people who rent don't, and then buying wins by default, as forced saving.

### Questions that matter as much as the numbers

1. **Will I live here at least 7–10 years?** Buying and selling within a few years usually loses money to costs.
2. **Is the EMI under about a third of take-home pay,** with the emergency fund intact (Module 5)?
3. **Is the property legally clean?** Title, encumbrance, approvals; for builder projects, **K-RERA registration**, which you can search on the K-RERA website ([K-RERA](https://rera.kerala.gov.in/)).
4. **Does it fit my other goals?** A house that stops retirement saving is too expensive.

### Tax, briefly

Under the old regime, home loan principal and stamp duty count within section 123 (FIN-M10-L02) and interest has its own deduction within limits; the new regime mostly doesn't give these for a home you live in. Don't let tax decide the house.

## Local example

**Rahul** was offered a 2BHK flat near Vatakara for ₹42 lakh by a builder. His family urged him to buy "before prices go up". He ran the rent-or-buy sheet with three sets of assumptions and asked two questions first.

**Will he stay 10 years?** His department can transfer him across the district or beyond. Probably not.
**Is the project on K-RERA?** He searched the K-RERA site: it was registered, with an expected completion date two years away.

The EMI would be about ₹29,159, almost all of his take-home pay. His numbers showed renting and investing ahead in two of three scenarios, and buying ahead only if prices rose fast. He decided to wait: keep renting near his office, build his down payment in a mix of safe and growth investments per his IPS, and revisit in three years when his pay and posting are clearer. "Waiting isn't losing," he wrote. "Buying a house I can't afford would be."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala Real Estate Regulatory Authority (K-RERA)](https://rera.kerala.gov.in/) | K-RERA: search a project's registration and see how complaints work | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Angel One: no prepayment charges on floating-rate loans from 1 January 2026](https://www.angelone.in/news/personal-finance/rbi-new-rule-no-prepayment-penalty-on-floating-loans-from-jan-1-2026) | No prepayment charges on individuals' floating-rate home loans from 2026 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 9, "Time Value of Money III: Unequal Multiple Payment Values": skim how uneven cash flows are compared | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Write your honest answers to the four questions for your situation (or for your family's next house decision).
2. Build the rent-or-buy calculator from the template with your own or realistic local numbers: price, down payment, costs, loan rate and term, rent.
3. Run at least three scenarios: low, middle and high house price growth, with matching investment returns.
4. Check the EMI as a share of your take-home pay and against your other goals.
5. If a specific project is involved, search for it on K-RERA and note its registration details.
6. Write your decision (buy now, buy later with a date, or rent) and the reasons.

**Proof to record:** Your rent-or-buy calculator with three scenarios, the four answers and your written decision, saved in 11 Big goals.

## Template: rent or buy calculator (yearly version)

```
INPUTS: B2 price  B3 down % (0.2)  B4 buying costs % (0.08)  B5 loan rate  B6 loan years  B7 upkeep per year
        B8 rent per month now  B9 rent growth (0.05)  B10 house growth  B11 investment return  B12 years to compare (10)
B14: loan        =B2*(1-B3)
B15: EMI         =PMT(B5/12,B6*12,-B14)
B16: loan left after B12 years   =-FV(B5/12,B12*12,-B15,B14)
B17: BUY wealth  =B2*(1+B10)^B12-B16
RENT path (one row per year, years 1..B12 in A20:A29):
B20: rent this year     =$B$8*12*(1+$B$9)^(A20-1)
C20: owning cost        =$B$15*12+$B$7
D20: invested this year =MAX(C20-B20,0)
E20: investment value   =(E19+D20)*(1+$B$11)     (E19 = starting amount: =B2*(B3+B4))
B30: RENT wealth  =E29
(The yearly version is simpler than monthly; results are close.)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Comparing EMI with rent only.** Include the down payment's lost returns, buying costs, upkeep and what you would invest when renting.
- **Assuming prices always rise fast.** Test low-growth scenarios. Some areas stay flat for years.
- **Buying before job location is stable.** Transfers and job changes turn a dream home into a burden.
- **Skipping legal checks.** Check title, encumbrance and K-RERA registration before paying any advance.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does the "rent and invest" path assume?
    - A) House prices fall
    - B) You invest the down payment and the monthly difference every month
    - C) Rent never rises
    - D) You spend the difference
2. Where can you check whether a builder's project in Kerala is registered?
    - A) Your bank passbook
    - B) The builder's brochure
    - C) A WhatsApp group
    - D) The K-RERA website
3. Why does living in a place only a few years usually favour renting?
    - A) Banks refuse short loans
    - B) Rent is always cheaper
    - C) Houses lose value in 3 years
    - D) Buying and selling costs eat into any gain over a short period
4. In the worked example, what changed which option won?
    - A) The assumptions for house price growth and investment returns
    - B) Nothing; buying always wins
    - C) The colour of the house
    - D) The bank's name

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** K-RERA project search, the prepayment rule and OpenStax chapter 9's overview
- **Action:** Run a rent-or-buy comparison with three scenarios and write your decision. It is done when your proof is saved: your rent-or-buy calculator with three scenarios, the four answers and your written decision, saved in 11 Big goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Renting builds wealth only if the money saved is actually invested.
2. **D.** K-RERA lets you search registered projects and file complaints.
3. **D.** Stamp duty, registration and selling costs need years of growth to recover.
4. **A.** Test several scenarios because the future is unknown.

sections.title: FIN-M11-L03: Children's education
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Estimate the future cost of a child's education, choose a saving mix by time horizon, and plan how loans and scholarships fit without sacrificing your retirement. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Education is the goal Kerala families care about most, and costs can rise faster than general inflation. A plan made early turns a frightening number into a monthly habit.

### Step 1: the future cost

Pick a realistic course (engineering, medicine, nursing, a degree plus coaching) and find **today's total cost**: fees for all years, hostel, books, travel. Then grow it to the year it starts. This course uses **7% a year** for education in examples; it is an assumption, not a forecast.

**Worked example:** a course costing ₹8,00,000 in total today, starting in 12 years, at 7% education inflation, will cost about **₹18,01,753**. Saving for it at an assumed 8% a year needs about **₹7,491 a month** for 12 years (=PMT(0.08/12, 144, 0, -1801753)).

### Step 2: the saving mix, by time horizon

- **More than 7 years away:** a larger growth share is reasonable (Module 8), such as equity index funds, plus safe options. As the date nears, move money step by step to safe options so a market fall in the last years can't wreck the plan.
- **Sukanya Samriddhi (SSA)** for a daughter: **8.2%** in October to December 2026, ₹250 to ₹1.5 lakh a year, deposits for 15 years ([rates](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/), [limits](https://www.outlookmoney.com/retirement/invest/fd-small-savings/post-office-small-savings-schemes-know-the-interest-rates-and-key-features), check current rules). Government-backed and tax-free interest, but money is locked; it suits part of a daughter's education and marriage plan.
- **PPF** (FIN-M09-L04): safe and tax-free, with a 15-year term.
- **3 years or less away:** safe options only.

### Step 3: loans and scholarships are part of the plan

You don't have to fund every rupee in advance. **Education loans** exist; under **PM-Vidyalaxmi**, students at eligible institutions can get collateral-free, guarantor-free loans, with interest subvention for families earning up to ₹8 lakh on loans up to ₹10 lakh ([PIB](https://education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/PIB2071134.pdf), check current rules). Merit and need-based scholarships help too. Plan to fund, say, 60–80% and leave room for these.

### Step 4: don't sacrifice retirement

There are loans for education; there are no loans for retirement. A common saying among planners is "fix your own oxygen mask first". If money is tight, keep your retirement saving going (Module 12) and fund education with what remains, plus loans and scholarships if needed.

### Involve the child, when old enough

A teenager who knows the family's budget makes different choices: a government college, an entrance coaching that fits, a part-time job. Money talk is part of education too.

## Local example

**Nisha**, who runs Nisha's Oven, has a daughter, Ammu, aged 6. Nisha wanted Ammu to have the choice of a professional course in 12 years. She estimated today's cost of a four-year course with hostel at ₹8 lakh, which grows to about ₹18,01,753 at 7%.

Her plan: ₹3,000 a month into SSA for Ammu (safe, tax-free, locked), and ₹4,000 a month into an equity index fund through a SIP (after writing her Investment Policy Statement), moving it step by step to safe options from Ammu's age 15. Together, at her assumed returns, they cover about 80% of the estimate; the rest can come from a scholarship, an education loan or her savings at the time.

She kept her own retirement contribution (₹2,500 a month) running alongside. "Ammu will have choices," she said, "and I won't be a burden on her later."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Indian Bank: small savings interest rates, October to December 2026](https://indianbank.bank.in/departments/interest-rates-for-small-savings-schemes/) | The current Sukanya Samriddhi rate | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Outlook Money: post office schemes, deposit limits and features (January 2024)](https://www.outlookmoney.com/retirement/invest/fd-small-savings/post-office-small-savings-schemes-know-the-interest-rates-and-key-features) | SSA and PPF deposit limits and terms | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [PIB: PM-Vidyalaxmi education loan scheme approved (PDF, November 2024)](https://education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/PIB2071134.pdf) | PM-Vidyalaxmi: who is eligible and what support is available | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. If you have or plan children, choose one education goal per child (or for a younger sibling or niece/nephew you support, or a future child).
2. Find today's total cost of a realistic course, from college websites or families who have done it.
3. Calculate the future cost and monthly saving with the template.
4. Choose the saving mix by horizon and write when you will move money to safe options.
5. Write what share you plan to cover from savings, and the backup: loans, scholarships.
6. No children and no plans? Write "not applicable now" and calculate the example for practice.

**Proof to record:** Your education goal calculation, saving mix and backup plan (or the practice calculation), saved in 11 Big goals.

## Template: education goal

```
B2: child's name / goal             B3: years until the course starts
B4: total cost today (₹)            B5: education inflation (e.g. 0.07)
B6: future cost (₹)                 =B4*(1+B5)^B3
B7: share to fund from savings      (e.g. 0.8)
B8: target (₹)                      =B6*B7
B9: assumed return while saving     (e.g. 0.08; lower it as the date nears)
B10: monthly saving (₹)             =PMT(B9/12,B3*12,0,-B8)
Glide path: from (year) ____ move ___% a year to safe options.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Guessing the cost.** Use real fee lists and add hostel, books and travel.
- **Keeping education money in equity until the last year.** Move it to safe options gradually in the final 3–5 years.
- **Stopping retirement saving for education.** Education can be partly borrowed; retirement can't.
- **Buying an "education insurance plan" without calculating its return.** Check any bundled plan with the RATE method from FIN-M07-L01.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. A course costs ₹8 lakh today, starting in 12 years, at 7% inflation. About how much will it cost?
    - A) About ₹8.6 lakh
    - B) About ₹18 lakh
    - C) About ₹40 lakh
    - D) About ₹12 lakh
2. What was the Sukanya Samriddhi interest rate for October to December 2026?
    - A) 8.2%
    - B) 6.7%
    - C) 7.1%
    - D) 4%
3. Why move education savings to safe options in the last few years?
    - A) Safe options always earn more
    - B) Equity funds close after 10 years
    - C) It is required by law
    - D) A market fall close to the date could leave too little time to recover
4. If money is tight, what should usually continue alongside education saving?
    - A) A new car loan
    - B) Expensive coaching for every subject
    - C) Nothing else
    - D) Your own retirement saving

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The SSA rate and limits and the PM-Vidyalaxmi scheme
- **Action:** Calculate one education goal's future cost and monthly saving and write the saving mix and backup plan. It is done when your proof is saved: your education goal calculation, saving mix and backup plan (or the practice calculation), saved in 11 Big goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** ₹8,00,000 × 1.07¹² ≈ ₹18 lakh.
2. **A.** SSA was at 8.2% (check current rates).
3. **D.** The goal date is fixed; protect the money as it nears.
4. **D.** Education can be partly funded by loans and scholarships; retirement can't.

sections.title: FIN-M11-L04: Supporting your parents
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Map your parents' finances with them, close the most dangerous gaps (health cover, emergencies, scams), and agree how support is shared among siblings. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

In Kerala, many parents live on small pensions, savings, farm income or help from children, and Kerala's population is older than India's on average. Supporting parents is a value for most families. It works best with **a plan made together**, not with emergencies handled alone.

### Step 1: the parents' money map

With your parents' permission, write down:

- **Income:** pension, interest, rent, farm income, support from children
- **Savings and where they are:** banks, post office, co-operative societies, chitties, gold
- **Insurance and schemes:** health cover, KASP or Medisep eligibility (FIN-M07-L04)
- **Debts:** gold loans, family loans
- **Documents and nominees:** where the papers are, who the nominees are (Module 13)
- **Monthly expenses,** especially medicines

### Step 2: close the dangerous gaps first

1. **Health cover:** the biggest risk for older parents. Check scheme eligibility (KASP, Medisep if a parent is a government pensioner), existing policies and options for seniors (FIN-M07-L03). Note that Ayushman Vaya Vandana was reported as not implemented in Kerala as of November 2025 ([Onmanorama](https://www.onmanorama.com/lifestyle/health/2025/11/13/kerala-senior-citizens-health-insurance-options.amp.html)); check its current status.
2. **An emergency fund for parents,** even small, kept where they or you can reach it quickly.
3. **Regular income from savings:** safe options such as SCSS (for 60+, 8.2% in October to December 2026) and MIS, rather than one large co-operative deposit (FIN-M09-L03).
4. **Scam protection:** older people are targeted by "digital arrest", KYC and lottery frauds. Share the fraud response card (FIN-M04-L02) and Module 15.
5. **Nominations and documents:** check every account has a nominee and that someone knows where papers are.

### Step 3: share fairly among siblings

When several children support parents, money becomes a source of quiet resentment unless it is discussed. Agree: who contributes how much each month (by income, not equally), who handles which tasks (hospital visits, paperwork), and how big expenses will be shared. Write it down and review it yearly.

### Step 4: protect your own plan too

Support from a full emergency fund and a budget line, not from your retirement savings or a loan. If parents need more than you can give, look at schemes, siblings and their own assets (gold, land) before borrowing.

### Talking about money with parents

Start with care, not control: "I want to make sure you are protected if something happens." Ask questions, listen, and let them decide about their own money. A respectful conversation now prevents a frantic search for documents in a hospital corridor later.

## Local example

**Rahul** sat down with his parents and his sister on a Sunday. His father, a retired KSRTC conductor, drew a small pension; his mother had no income. Their money map showed: ₹3.5 lakh in a co-operative society, 11 pavan of gold (4 already pledged for an old loan), no private health insurance, and Rahul's father's pension papers in "the steel almirah, somewhere".

They agreed four things:

| Gap | Action | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Health cover | Check KASP eligibility at a hospital helpdesk; check whether his father's pension comes with any health scheme; compare a senior policy for his mother | Rahul |
| Gold loan | Repay it over 10 months from Rahul's budget line for parents, so the gold isn't auctioned | Rahul |
| Co-operative deposit | Confirm membership and the Kerala guarantee; move part to SCSS when the deposit matures | Father, with Rahul |
| Documents | Make one file with pension papers, bank passbooks and policies; check nominees | Sister |

Rahul contributes ₹5,000 a month and his sister, who earns less, ₹2,000; big medical costs are shared in the same proportion. They wrote it in a shared note and put a yearly review in December.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Onmanorama: health cover options for Kerala's senior citizens (November 2025)](https://www.onmanorama.com/lifestyle/health/2025/11/13/kerala-senior-citizens-health-insurance-options.amp.html) | Health cover options for seniors in Kerala, including KASP and the Karunya fund | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [India Post: saving schemes and current interest rates](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving) | SCSS and MIS rates for parents' regular income | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Kerala Police: 1930, the national cyber crime helpline](https://ps.keralapolice.gov.in/ernakulamruralcyber-ps/notifications/National-Cyber-Crime-Reporting-Helpline-No-1930-3338) | The 1930 helpline, to share with your parents | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Ask your parents for a money conversation, explaining why. Choose a calm time.
2. Fill in the parents' money map together, writing only what they are comfortable sharing.
3. Mark the dangerous gaps: health cover, emergency money, risky deposits, debts, missing nominees or documents.
4. Agree one action for each gap, with who does it and by when.
5. If you have siblings, agree contributions and tasks in writing.
6. Add the support to your own Budget tab as a planned line.

**Proof to record:** The parents' money map (with private numbers covered or left out), the gaps and actions, and any sibling agreement, saved in 11 Big goals.

## Template: parents' money map

```
Income (monthly): pension ____ interest ____ rent/farm ____ from children ____
Savings: bank ____ post office ____ co-op ____ chitty ____ gold (pavan) ____
Health cover: scheme ____ private policy ____ eligible for KASP? ____ Medisep (pensioners)? ____
Debts: ____
Documents kept at: ____   Nominees checked? ____
Monthly expenses: ____ of which medicines ____
Biggest worry (in their words): ____
```

## Template: sibling support agreement

```
Monthly contribution:  ____ ₹____   ____ ₹____   ____ ₹____
Big expenses (medical, repairs) shared in proportion: ___% / ___% / ___%
Tasks: hospital visits ____ paperwork ____ bills ____
Review every year in ____ (month)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Taking over without asking.** It is their money. Offer help; let them decide.
- **Waiting for a crisis to talk.** In a hospital corridor there is no time to find papers or compare options.
- **Funding parents from your retirement savings.** Use a budget line and an emergency fund; protect your own future too.
- **Unspoken sibling arrangements.** Write the agreement down. Clarity protects relationships.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is usually the biggest financial risk for older parents?
    - A) A large health expense
    - B) Too much gold
    - C) Low phone balance
    - D) A small electricity bill
2. Which scheme is meant for regular income for people aged 60 and above?
    - A) SCSS
    - B) SSA
    - C) KVP
    - D) ELSS
3. How should siblings share support fairly?
    - A) Agree contributions by ability and tasks in writing, and review yearly
    - B) Always equally, regardless of income
    - C) Never discuss it
    - D) Whoever lives closest pays everything
4. Where should support for parents come from in your own plan?
    - A) A planned budget line and your emergency fund
    - B) Your retirement savings
    - C) A loan app
    - D) A personal loan

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Kerala's senior health cover options, SCSS and MIS rates and the 1930 helpline
- **Action:** Make a money map with your parents, agree actions for the dangerous gaps and, if relevant, a sibling agreement. It is done when your proof is saved: the parents' money map (with private numbers covered or left out), the gaps and actions, and any sibling agreement, saved in 11 Big goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** Hospital costs can wipe out savings; health cover comes first.
2. **A.** The Senior Citizens Savings Scheme pays quarterly interest (8.2% in October to December 2026).
3. **A.** A written, fair agreement prevents resentment.
4. **A.** Protect your own future while you help.

sections.title: Module 12: Retirement and financial independence
sections.summary: Estimate how much you need to retire, what pensions will cover, and how much to save each month, and use the ideas of financial independence to see what a higher savings rate can buy you.
sections.content:
## Overview

Retirement is decades away for many learners, which is exactly why it matters now: time does most of the work (Module 8). This module turns a vague worry into a number, then into a monthly plan you can start small and raise every year.

You also compare the pension sources in India (government pensions, EPS, NPS, APY, annuities) and learn a simple bucket method for drawing money safely in retirement. FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) is explained honestly, with the cautions that matter in India. Your **Retirement** tab joins your final plan.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Estimate a retirement corpus from your own expenses with inflation and life expectancy
- Subtract expected pensions and find the level and step-up monthly saving
- Compare government pensions, EPS, NPS, APY and annuities
- Plan retirement withdrawals with the bucket method
- Calculate your years to financial independence and explain FIRE's India-specific cautions

## Time

About 5 hours in total: 4 hours of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: week 25.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M12-L01: How much is enough? Estimating your retirement corpus (about 2 hours)
2. FIN-M12-L02: Pension options, and financial independence (FIRE) (about 2 hours)

## Module project: My retirement estimate and plan

1. Complete the Retirement tab with cautious assumptions and your pension sources.
2. Choose your monthly retirement saving: a starting amount and a yearly step-up, and the accounts it goes to (from FIN-M09-L04).
3. Set up the standing instruction or SIP for the starting amount (even a small one), or write the date you will start.
4. Write your FIRE statement and your target savings rate.
5. Put "recalculate retirement" in your yearly review.

**Proof to record:** Your Retirement tab, the chosen saving plan with proof of the first contribution (or the start date) and your FIRE statement, saved in 12 Retirement.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expenses | A guess | Today's rupees only | Inflated to the retirement year, with health costs considered |
| Corpus | Not calculated | Calculated with optimistic numbers | Calculated with cautious assumptions and tested |
| Pensions | Ignored | Listed | Listed with rules and subtracted from the need |
| Saving plan | None | An amount | Starting amount, step-up and accounts, with the first contribution made |
| Independence | Not considered | Read about FIRE | Own years-to-FI calculated and a savings-rate target set |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Calculate your corpus with the Retirement tab (FIN-M12-L01, steps 2–5).
- Start any amount for retirement, even ₹500 a month, with a 10% yearly step-up.
- Check APY eligibility if you don't pay income tax.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Corpus formula (growing withdrawals) | E × (1 − ((1+g)/(1+r))^N) ÷ (r − g) × (1 + r). |
| Plan retirement to at least | Age 85, and test 90. |
| Step-up SIP | A SIP raised by a fixed % every year as income grows. |
| APY | Ages 18–40, non-taxpayers; guaranteed ₹1,000–5,000 a month from 60. |
| NPS exit (non-government) | Up to 80% lump sum, at least 20% annuity; full withdrawal if corpus ≤ ₹8 lakh. |
| FIRE target | 25–33 × yearly expenses (4%–3% withdrawal). |
| Bucket method | Safe money for 2–3 years, medium-term money for 3–10, growth for later; refill yearly. |
| Coast FIRE | Enough invested early to grow to your target by retirement with no more saving. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Leaving retirement for later.** Each decade of delay roughly doubles the monthly saving needed.
- **Assuming one scheme will cover everything.** Combine sources and plan your own corpus too.
- **Forgetting health costs.** Medical costs rise with age; keep insurance and a health buffer in the plan.

sections.title: FIN-M12-L01: How much is enough? Estimating your retirement corpus
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Estimate the retirement corpus you need from your own expenses, inflation and life expectancy, subtract expected pensions, and find the monthly saving, including a step-up plan. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Retirement is the longest goal you will ever fund: 20 to 30 years of living costs, with no salary. It is also the goal most often left "for later". This lesson gives you a number and a monthly plan, so later becomes now.

### Step 1: retirement expenses in today's rupees

Start from your current essential and comfortable spending (Module 3), then adjust: no work travel or EMIs, possibly no rent, but **higher health costs**. Many people use 70–100% of current spending; use your own judgement and keep health in mind.

### Step 2: grow it to your retirement year

> **Yearly expense at retirement = monthly expense today × 12 × (1 + inflation) ^ years to retirement**

### Step 3: the corpus that pays it for life

You need enough to pay a rising expense (inflation continues) for the whole retirement, while the remaining money earns a return. A formula for a growing payment at the start of each year:

> **Corpus = E × (1 − ((1 + g) ÷ (1 + r)) ^ N) ÷ (r − g) × (1 + r)**

where E = first year's expense, g = inflation, r = return during retirement, N = years in retirement. (If r and g are equal, the corpus is simply E × N.)

**Worked example** (Anu, made-up, all assumptions): ₹12,000 a month today, retiring at 60 in 33 years, inflation 5%, a 7% return during retirement, 25 years of retirement (to 85).

- First-year expense at 60: ₹1,44,000 × 1.05^33 = **₹7,20,459** a year.
- Corpus needed: about **₹1,44,95,334**, roughly 20 times the first year's expense.
- To reach it with a fixed monthly SIP at an assumed 8% a year for 33 years: about **₹7,447 a month**.

### Step 4: subtract what pensions will pay

Pensions reduce the corpus you must build: a government pension, EPS pension from EPF, an NPS annuity, Atal Pension Yojana (FIN-M12-L02). Convert each expected pension to a yearly amount at retirement and subtract it from E before calculating the corpus.

### Step 5: start where you are, and step up

₹7,447 a month may be impossible today on Anu's income. That is normal. A **step-up SIP** starts smaller and raises the amount every year as income grows (the raise rule from Module 1):

- Starting at ₹2,000 a month and raising it 10% a year for 33 years grows to about **₹1,37,62,501** at 8%.
- Starting at about **₹2,106** with 10% yearly increases reaches the full target.

### The honest caveats

Every number here depends on assumptions: inflation, returns, how long you live, health costs. Small changes move the answer a lot. So: use cautious assumptions, recalculate every year in your review, and treat the result as a direction, not a promise. The biggest risk isn't a wrong assumption; it is not starting.

### How long to plan for

Plan to at least 85, and test 90. Running out of money at 82 is far worse than leaving some behind.

## Local example

**Fathima**, 31, did the calculation for herself: ₹18,000 a month today (including higher health costs later), retiring at 60, inflation 5%, 7% in retirement, to 88. The corpus came to about ₹2.2 crore in future rupees. Her first reaction: "Impossible."

Then she broke it down. Her PPF and NPS (FIN-M09-L04) would cover part of it. A step-up plan starting at ₹3,500 a month and rising 10% a year was within reach of her average income. And two levers made a big difference: retiring at 62 instead of 60, and keeping some freelance work in her early sixties. Her final plan: ₹3,500 a month now (PPF ₹2,000 and NPS ₹1,500), raised every April, and a yearly recalculation. "It's a big number," she wrote, "but it's a number I can walk towards."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 8, "Time Value of Money II: Equal Multiple Payments": the sections on annuities and growing annuities | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The long-term planning and pension module | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Retirement** tab with the template.
2. Enter your monthly retirement expenses in today's rupees, your current age, retirement age and the age to plan to (at least 85).
3. Enter cautious assumptions: inflation, return before retirement, return during retirement. Write why you chose them.
4. Enter what you already have for retirement (EPF, PPF, NPS) and any expected pensions.
5. Read the corpus and the monthly saving needed, both level and with a yearly step-up.
6. Test two changes: retiring two years later, and a 1% lower return. Write how much each changes the answer.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Retirement tab with your assumptions, corpus, monthly saving (level and step-up) and the two tests, saved in 12 Retirement.

## Template: Retirement tab

```
INPUTS
B2: monthly expenses in retirement, today's ₹      B3: current age      B4: retirement age      B5: plan to age
B6: inflation (e.g. 0.05)    B7: return before retirement (e.g. 0.08)    B8: return in retirement (e.g. 0.07)
B9: retirement savings today (₹)    B10: expected yearly pensions at retirement, in today's ₹
CALCULATIONS
B12: years to retirement     =B4-B3
B13: years in retirement     =B5-B4
B14: first-year expense      =(B2*12-B10)*(1+B6)^B12
B15: corpus needed           =IF(B8=B6,B14*B13,B14*(1-((1+B6)/(1+B8))^B13)/(B8-B6)*(1+B8))
B16: today's savings grown   =B9*(1+B7)^B12
B17: still to build          =MAX(B15-B16,0)
B18: level monthly saving    =PMT(B7/12,B12*12,0,-B17,1)
STEP-UP CHECK (yearly table; A21 = year 1 ... ; C = monthly saving that year)
B21: starting monthly saving    C21: =B21    C22: =C21*1.10   (copy down for each year)
D21: value at year end          =FV($B$7/12,12,-C21,0,1)     D22: =D21*(1+$B$7/12)^12+FV($B$7/12,12,-C22,0,1)
Compare the last year's value with B17.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Planning retirement in today's rupees.** Inflate expenses to the retirement year; prices may be several times higher.
- **Planning to 75.** Plan to at least 85 and test 90.
- **Using optimistic returns.** Use cautious returns; a plan that works with lower returns is a strong plan.
- **Waiting for a bigger income.** Start small and step up; time matters more than the starting amount.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why must retirement expenses be inflated to the retirement year?
    - A) Prices will be much higher by then
    - B) Expenses fall after retirement
    - C) Banks require it
    - D) It doesn't matter
2. In the formula, what happens to the corpus if the return in retirement equals inflation?
    - A) Corpus = first-year expense × years in retirement
    - B) Corpus = 0
    - C) Corpus doubles
    - D) The formula can't be used at all
3. What is a step-up SIP?
    - A) A SIP that increases by a fixed percentage every year
    - B) A loan for investing
    - C) A tax-saving deposit
    - D) A SIP that stops after a year
4. To what age should a retirement plan usually run, at least?
    - A) 70
    - B) 85, and test 90
    - C) Retirement age only
    - D) 65

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapter 8 on annuities and the NCFE long-term planning module
- **Action:** Build your Retirement tab, estimate your corpus and monthly saving, and test two changes. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Retirement tab with your assumptions, corpus, monthly saving (level and step-up) and the two tests, saved in 12 Retirement.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** At 5% inflation, prices more than quadruple in 30 years.
2. **A.** With zero real return, you simply need N years of expenses.
3. **A.** It starts smaller and grows with your income.
4. **B.** Running out of money late in life is the worst outcome.

sections.title: FIN-M12-L02: Pension options, and financial independence (FIRE)
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare the main pension sources in India, plan how to draw money in retirement, and understand FIRE with your own years-to-independence calculation. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Where retirement income can come from

| Source | Who | What it gives | As of |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Government pension | Government employees under the old pension or as decided for their scheme | Monthly pension with dearness relief (Module 14) | Check your scheme |
| EPS pension (part of EPF) | EPF members | A monthly pension based on service and salary rules | Check with EPFO |
| NPS annuity and lump sum | NPS subscribers | Non-government: up to 80% lump sum and at least 20% to buy an annuity at normal exit; full withdrawal if the corpus is ₹8 lakh or less | December 2025 rules |
| Atal Pension Yojana (APY) | Ages 18–40 with a bank or post office account; not for income-tax payers (from October 2022) | Guaranteed ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 a month from 60, then to the spouse, then the corpus to the nominee | PFRDA FAQs |
| Your own corpus | Everyone | PPF, deposits, SCSS (after 60), mutual funds, rent | Module 9 |

Sources: [NPS exit rules](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/personal-finance/pfrda-allows-financial-assistance-against-nps-corpus-under-exit-rule-tweaks-125121601190_1.html), [PFRDA APY FAQs](https://pfrda.org.in/web/pfrda/w/faqs/atal-pension-yojana), [SCSS rate](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving); check current rules.

**APY** is valuable for informal workers and low earners who don't pay income tax: small monthly contributions by auto-debit, a **guaranteed** pension amount. Its fixed pension doesn't rise with inflation, so it is a base, not the whole plan.

**Annuities** (the NPS annuity, or ones bought from insurers) turn a lump sum into a lifelong income. Most pay a fixed amount, which inflation erodes; compare the rates and options (with or without return of the purchase price to nominees) before choosing.

### Drawing money in retirement: the bucket idea

A simple way to manage a retirement corpus:

1. **Bucket 1, the next 2–3 years of expenses:** savings, FDs, SCSS and MIS (safe, income).
2. **Bucket 2, years 3–10:** debt options and some balanced investments.
3. **Bucket 3, after 10 years:** growth investments, to keep up with inflation.

Refill bucket 1 from the others once a year, taking from whichever has grown. This protects you from **selling growth investments in a crash** in the early years, the most damaging risk for new retirees.

### FIRE: Financial Independence, Retire Early

FIRE is a movement built on one idea: if your investments can pay your expenses for life, work becomes optional. Its common rule of thumb: you are financially independent when your investments reach about **25 to 33 times your yearly expenses** (a withdrawal rate of 4% to 3% a year). People who follow FIRE save 40–70% of income.

**The savings rate decides the timeline.** With a 5% real return and a 25× target, starting from zero:

| Savings rate | Years to financial independence |
| --- | --- |
| 10% | about 51 years |
| 20% | about 37 years |
| 30% | about 28 years |
| 40% | about 22 years |
| 50% | about 17 years |
| 60% | about 12 years |

Variants: **Lean FIRE** (a frugal life), **Fat FIRE** (a comfortable one), **Coast FIRE** (save enough early that it grows to your retirement corpus by 60 with no further saving, then only cover current expenses), **Barista FIRE** (part-time work covers part of expenses).

**India-specific cautions:** health insurance without an employer (Module 7), inflation that has often been higher than in the countries where FIRE began, family responsibilities (parents, weddings, education), and the need to plan for 40+ years of retirement if you stop early.

Even if early retirement isn't your aim, the FIRE maths is useful: **a higher savings rate shortens every goal**, and "financial independence" can mean the freedom to choose work you like, take a break or survive a job loss.

**Worked example (Coast FIRE):** Anu's corpus target of ₹1,44,95,334 at 60 would be reached, at an assumed 8% a year, from about **₹11,43,521 invested today** with nothing more added. She is far from that, but each ₹1 lakh she invests at 27 grows to about ₹12,67,605 by 60 at that rate.

## Local example

**Rahul** has a government job, so his retirement is partly covered by his pension scheme (Module 14), but the scheme's future is uncertain in Kerala as of 2026, so he planned as if it might give less than hoped. He added a personal corpus: NPS contributions through his job plus a small equity SIP.

His colleague **Joby**, 32, a software tester in Kozhikode, is attracted to FIRE. He earns well and lives with his parents. His savings rate is 45%, so the table suggests about 19 years to independence: around 51. Rahul asked him the India questions: health cover after leaving his job? His parents' care? A wedding? Joby added a family floater plus super top-up to his plan, kept his target at 33× expenses (a 3% withdrawal rate) instead of 25×, and called it "FI at 50, then choose".

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [PFRDA: Atal Pension Yojana FAQs](https://pfrda.org.in/web/pfrda/w/faqs/atal-pension-yojana) | Atal Pension Yojana: who can join, pension amounts, what happens after death, exit | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Business Standard: new NPS exit and withdrawal rules (December 2025)](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/personal-finance/pfrda-allows-financial-assistance-against-nps-corpus-under-exit-rule-tweaks-125121601190_1.html) | NPS exit and annuity rules from December 2025 | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Protean (NPS record-keeper): NPS withdrawal changes and tax](https://proteantech.in/articles/nps-withdrawal-rules-2025-changes-december/) | Tax on the NPS lump sum | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [Zerodha Varsity: all modules](https://zerodha.com/varsity/modules/) | Module 17, "NPS: National Pension System": the chapters on exit and annuities | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. List every pension source you have or can expect, with the rules from this lesson. Add their expected yearly amounts to your Retirement tab.
2. If you (or a parent or relative under 40) don't pay income tax, check whether APY fits, and write the decision.
3. Write your future bucket plan: what goes in each bucket at retirement.
4. Calculate your own years to financial independence with the template, using your savings rate from Module 2.
5. Write your position on FIRE in two sentences: what independence means for you, and the age or savings rate you are aiming for.

**Proof to record:** Your pension sources list, bucket plan, years-to-FI calculation and FIRE statement, saved in 12 Retirement.

## Template: years to financial independence

```
B2: yearly expenses (₹)            B3: yearly savings (₹)
B4: investments today (₹)          B5: real return (e.g. 0.05)
B6: multiple (25 = 4% withdrawal, 33 = 3%)
B7: FI target (₹)                  =B2*B6
B8: years to FI                    =NPER(B5,-B3,-B4,B7)
B9: savings rate %                 =B3/(B2+B3)*100
Coast check: amount needed today to reach the target in N years at return r:  =B7/(1+r)^N
```

## Template: bucket plan at retirement

```
Bucket 1 (years 1-3): ₹____ in ____ (savings, FDs, SCSS, MIS)
Bucket 2 (years 3-10): ₹____ in ____
Bucket 3 (10+ years): ₹____ in ____
Refill rule: once a year, top up Bucket 1 from ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Relying on one pension source.** Schemes change; combine a pension, your own corpus and safe income options.
- **Treating a fixed annuity as inflation-proof.** A fixed pension buys less every year; keep growth assets for later years.
- **Copying FIRE numbers from other countries.** Use Indian inflation, health and family costs, and a cautious withdrawal rate.
- **Selling growth investments in a crash early in retirement.** The bucket method keeps 2–3 years of expenses safe so you never have to.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Who can join the Atal Pension Yojana, as of November 2026?
    - A) Anyone over 60
    - B) Only income-tax payers
    - C) People aged 18–40 with a bank or post office account who don't pay income tax
    - D) Only government employees
2. What does the FIRE rule of thumb of 25× yearly expenses correspond to?
    - A) A 25% withdrawal rate
    - B) A 4% yearly withdrawal rate
    - C) A 25% savings rate
    - D) Retiring at 25
3. Why keep 2–3 years of expenses in safe options in retirement?
    - A) Banks require it
    - B) So you never have to sell growth investments in a crash
    - C) They earn the most
    - D) To avoid all tax
4. According to the table, about how long to financial independence at a 50% savings rate?
    - A) About 51 years
    - B) About 17 years
    - C) About 5 years
    - D) Never

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** APY rules, NPS exit and tax rules, and Varsity's NPS chapters on exit
- **Action:** List your pension sources, write a bucket plan and calculate your years to financial independence. It is done when your proof is saved: your pension sources list, bucket plan, years-to-FI calculation and FIRE statement, saved in 12 Retirement.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Income-tax payers can't join from 1 October 2022 (check current rules).
2. **B.** 1 ÷ 25 = 4%.
3. **B.** Selling after a crash early in retirement does lasting damage.
4. **B.** Higher savings rates shorten the path sharply.

Save it in your Money Folder and paste its link (or a short note of where it is) in this task's note. Never paste account numbers, passwords or OTPs anywhere.

sections.title: Module 13: Estate basics: nominations, wills and documents
sections.summary: Make sure your money reaches the right people with the least trouble if something happens to you: nominations on every account, a will when you need one, and a family money file that tells your family where everything is.
sections.content:
## Overview

Estate planning sounds like something for old or wealthy people. It isn't. A missing nominee, a nominee who has died, or a family that doesn't know an account exists turns a sad time into months of visits and paperwork, and money can end up unclaimed for years.

This module uses the new rules: up to four nominees for bank deposits from November 2025, up to three for demat and mutual funds from September 2026, and RBI's UDGAM portal for finding unclaimed deposits. You audit every nomination, build a document register and family money file, and decide on a will. The result is part of your final plan.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain what nominees and joint holders can and can't do
- Apply the 2025–2026 nomination rules for banks, lockers, demat and mutual funds
- Find unclaimed deposits with UDGAM
- Know the basic requirements for a valid will and when to use a lawyer
- Build a document register and family money file, without passwords

## Time

About 4 hours in total: 3 hours of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: week 26.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M13-L01: Nominations and joint accounts (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. FIN-M13-L02: Wills and your family money file (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Module project: My document system and nomination audit

1. Complete the nomination audit for every account and policy, with all urgent updates done.
2. Complete the document register and fetch your key documents into DigiLocker.
3. Finish the family money file and give its location to a trusted person.
4. Write your will decision: made, booked with a lawyer, or the trigger event for making one.
5. Add "nominations, money file and will" to your yearly review checklist.

**Proof to record:** Screenshots of the nomination audit and document register, confirmation that the money file exists and who knows where it is, and your will decision, saved in 13 Estate.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nominations | Unknown | Some checked | Every account checked and urgent updates done |
| Rules | Unaware | Know the bank rule | Know the bank, locker and demat/MF rules as of 2026 |
| Documents | Scattered | Listed | Register complete; key documents in DigiLocker |
| Money file | None | Started | Complete, without passwords, and a trusted person knows where it is |
| Will | Not considered | Thought about | Made, booked or a clear trigger written |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Check and fix nominees on your main bank account and any insurance policy (FIN-M13-L01).
- Fetch Aadhaar and PAN into DigiLocker (FIN-M13-L02).
- Write a one-page money file and tell one person where it is.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Bank deposit nominees from 1 November 2025 | Up to four, simultaneous (shares adding to 100%) or successive. |
| Lockers and safe custody | Successive nomination only. |
| Demat and mutual fund nominees from 1 September 2026 | Up to three; single holders must nominate or opt out. |
| UDGAM | RBI's portal to search unclaimed deposits; claim at the bank. |
| Valid will basics | Adult of sound mind, signed, attested by two witnesses; registration optional. |
| Marriage and an old will | Under the Indian Succession Act, marriage revokes an earlier will. |
| Family money file | Where everything is and who to call, without passwords. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Leaving nominations from years ago unchecked.** People die, marry and fall out; nominations should follow your life.
- **Keeping everything in your head.** If only you know where things are, your family will struggle.
- **Waiting for "later" to make a will.** Make one when you have dependants or property, and update it after big changes.
